googleIndexChecker.question: How do I check if a URL is indexed by Google?
googleIndexChecker.answer: Paste the URL into the checker above and run it. We query Google for that exact page and tell you whether it's indexed, along with the title and snippet Google shows. You can also run a site:yourdomain.com/page search in Google yourself, but this tool additionally flags title rewrites and canonical drift.

googleIndexChecker.question: What does it mean when a page is submitted but not indexed?
googleIndexChecker.answer: It means you submitted the URL through a sitemap or Search Console, but Google has chosen not to index it yet. It usually points to thin or duplicate content, a canonical aimed at another URL, or a quality bar the page hasn't cleared.

googleIndexChecker.question: How long does Google take to index a page?
googleIndexChecker.answer: Anywhere from a few hours to a few weeks. New pages on established, well-linked sites are often indexed within days, while pages on new sites or with weak internal linking can take much longer. Requesting indexing in Search Console can speed it up.

googleIndexChecker.question: Why is my page crawled but not indexed?
googleIndexChecker.answer: Google fetched the page but decided it wasn't worth indexing — typically because the content is thin, duplicates another page, or offers little unique value. Improving depth and uniqueness, then requesting indexing, is the usual fix.

googleIndexChecker.question: What's the difference between crawled and indexed?
googleIndexChecker.answer: Crawled means Googlebot fetched the page. Indexed means Google stored it and is willing to show it in results. A page must be crawled before it can be indexed, but being crawled doesn't guarantee indexing.

googleIndexChecker.question: Can I check multiple URLs at once?
googleIndexChecker.answer: Yes. Switch to multiple-URL mode, paste up to 20 URLs (one per line), and check them in a single run. You get a compact table with each URL's status and can export the results as CSV.

googleIndexChecker.question: Is this checker really free?
googleIndexChecker.answer: Yes — it's completely free, with no sign-up and no Search Console connection. Paste any URL, yours or a competitor's, and check it.

schemaMarkupGenerator.question: Is JSON-LD better than Microdata or RDFa?
schemaMarkupGenerator.answer: For most sites, yes. JSON-LD is the format Google recommends because it sits in one tidy block in the head, separate from your HTML, which makes it easier to add, read and maintain than inline Microdata or RDFa.

schemaMarkupGenerator.question: Will schema markup boost my rankings?
schemaMarkupGenerator.answer: Schema isn't a direct ranking factor, but it helps search engines understand your content and can earn rich results that lift click-through rate. Better understanding and more clicks often lead to better performance over time.

schemaMarkupGenerator.question: Will this guarantee I get a rich result?
schemaMarkupGenerator.answer: No tool can. Valid markup makes your page eligible, but Google decides whether to show a rich result based on quality, content and its own systems. Filling the recommended fields improves your odds.

schemaMarkupGenerator.question: Do I need to keep this generator open for my schema to keep working?
schemaMarkupGenerator.answer: No. The generator just produces the code. Once you paste the script block into your page, the schema lives on your site and works on its own — you can close this tab.

schemaMarkupGenerator.question: Do I need schema markup on every page?
schemaMarkupGenerator.answer: Not necessarily, but it helps on any page with a clear type — articles, products, FAQs, your homepage. Mark up the pages that matter most first, then expand from there.

schemaMarkupGenerator.question: How do I test my structured data?
schemaMarkupGenerator.answer: Use Google's Rich Results Test or the Schema Markup Validator. Paste your code or enter the live URL and they'll confirm it's valid and show which rich results it's eligible for. The Test in Google button opens it for you.

schemaMarkupGenerator.question: Is this generator really free?
schemaMarkupGenerator.answer: Yes — completely free, with no signup. Generate as many schema blocks as you need. If you'd rather have schema added to every page automatically, that's what BLG does for you.

jsonldSchema.question: What is JSON-LD Schema?
jsonldSchema.answer: JSON-LD Schema is a structured data format that helps search engines and LLMs better understand your website content. It provides context about your pages by marking up information like business details, products, articles, FAQs, and more in a format that machines can easily process.

jsonldSchema.question: How does the free JSON-LD Schema generator work?
jsonldSchema.answer: Our tool analyzes your website content and automatically generates the appropriate JSON-LD Schema markup for your pages. It identifies your content type, extracts relevant information, and formats it according to schema.org standards, ready for you to implement on your website.

jsonldSchema.question: What impact does JSON-LD Schema have on my website?
jsonldSchema.answer: Implementing JSON-LD Schema can significantly improve how your website appears in search results with rich snippets, enhance visibility in LLMs like ChatGPT and Perplexity, and potentially boost click-through rates. It helps search engines understand your content better, which can lead to improved rankings.

jsonldSchema.question: What types of schema does your tool support and which are most common?
jsonldSchema.answer: Our tool supports a wide range of schema types including Organization, LocalBusiness, Person, Product, Article, BlogPosting, FAQPage, Event, Recipe, and more. The most common schemas are: Organization/LocalBusiness (for business websites), Product (for e-commerce), Article/BlogPosting (for content sites), and FAQPage (for FAQ sections). Each schema type serves a specific purpose - business schemas establish entity information, Product schema enables rich product listings, Article schema helps content appear in news carousels, and FAQ schema can generate rich snippets with expandable question in search results.

jsonldSchema.question: Can I verify my implementation?
jsonldSchema.answer: Yes, navigate to https://search.google.com/test/rich-results OR https://validator.schema.org/ to verify your implementation.

jsonldSchema.question: Can JSON-LD Schema hurt my website?
jsonldSchema.answer: When implemented correctly, JSON-LD Schema will not hurt your website. However, incorrect implementation or using spammy markup could potentially lead to penalties. Our tool ensures your schema is properly formatted and follows best practices to avoid any negative impacts.

jsonldSchema.question: Do I need technical knowledge to implement JSON-LD Schema?
jsonldSchema.answer: No technical expertise is required with our tool. We generate the complete JSON-LD code that you can simply copy and paste into your website. If you use a CMS like WordPress, you can easily add it using plugins or by pasting it into your header section.

jsonldSchema.question: How often should I update my JSON-LD Schema?
jsonldSchema.answer: You should update your JSON-LD Schema whenever you make significant changes to your website content, products, or business information. It's also good practice to review your schema periodically to ensure it remains accurate and up-to-date with the latest schema.org standards.

jsonldSchema.question: Where can I learn more about JSON-LD Schema?
jsonldSchema.answer: Best way is to navigate to the the official schema.org website.

canonicalChecker.question: What is a canonical tag?
canonicalChecker.answer: A canonical tag (rel="canonical") tells search engines which version of a page is the "original." It prevents duplicate content penalties when similar or identical pages exist across your site. For example, if the same content is accessible via multiple URLs, the canonical tag signals which one should be indexed and ranked.

canonicalChecker.question: Should every page have a canonical tag?
canonicalChecker.answer: Yes. Every indexable page should have a self-referencing canonical tag. This is considered an SEO best practice even if no duplicates exist. It proactively prevents issues that can arise from URL parameters, session IDs, or syndicated content creating unintended duplicate pages.

canonicalChecker.question: What happens if the canonical tag is missing?
canonicalChecker.answer: Without a canonical tag, search engines must guess which version of a page to index. This can lead to diluted ranking signals and duplicate content issues. Google may choose a version you don't prefer, splitting link equity and potentially hurting your rankings.

canonicalChecker.question: Can canonical tags hurt SEO?
canonicalChecker.answer: Yes, if misconfigured. Pointing a canonical to the wrong URL can cause Google to ignore your preferred page entirely. Common mistakes include canonicalizing to a non-existent page, pointing to a different domain, or having multiple conflicting canonical tags on the same page.

canonicalChecker.question: What is the difference between a canonical tag and a redirect?
canonicalChecker.answer: A canonical tag is a suggestion to search engines about which URL to index, while a 301 redirect physically moves users and bots to a different URL. Use redirects for permanent URL changes and canonicals for duplicate content where you want to keep both URLs accessible but consolidate ranking signals.

sitemap.question: What is an XML sitemap?
sitemap.answer: An XML sitemap is a file that lists the important URLs on your website so search engines can discover and crawl them more efficiently. It typically lives at /sitemap.xml and can also include metadata like last-modified dates, change frequency, and image references. Sitemaps are especially valuable for new sites, large sites, or sites with deep content hierarchies.

sitemap.question: Do I need a sitemap if my site is small?
sitemap.answer: Even small sites benefit from having a sitemap. While Google can usually discover pages through internal links on well-structured small sites, a sitemap ensures nothing is missed — especially isolated pages, recently published blog posts, or content deep in your site structure. It's a low-effort safeguard that can speed up indexing.

sitemap.question: What's the maximum number of URLs per sitemap?
sitemap.answer: Google recommends no more than 50,000 URLs per sitemap file, and the file should be smaller than 50MB uncompressed. If your site has more URLs, you should split them into multiple sitemap files and reference all of them from a single sitemap index file.

sitemap.question: What is a sitemap index?
sitemap.answer: A sitemap index is a special XML file that references multiple sitemap files. It's used when a single sitemap would exceed the 50,000 URL limit or when you want to organize URLs by content type (e.g., a blog sitemap, a product sitemap, and an image sitemap). The sitemap index itself contains 0 URL entries, only pointers to other sitemaps — that's expected, not an error.

sitemap.question: Why does my sitemap show cross-domain URLs as a warning?
sitemap.answer: Search engines like Google only trust a sitemap for URLs on the same domain as the sitemap file itself. If your sitemap at example.com/sitemap.xml lists URLs on other-site.com, Google will ignore those entries. Cross-domain URLs are usually a sign of a misconfigured CMS, a copy-paste mistake, or improperly handled subdomains.

sitemap.question: Where should my sitemap be located?
sitemap.answer: The standard location is /sitemap.xml at the root of your domain (e.g., https://example.com/sitemap.xml). You should also reference it inside your robots.txt file using a line like 'Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml' so crawlers can discover it automatically.

sitemap.question: Does Google index every URL in my sitemap?
sitemap.answer: Not automatically. A sitemap tells search engines which pages exist, but Google still decides whether each URL is worth indexing based on content quality, duplication, crawl budget, and other signals. Including a URL in the sitemap improves its chances of being crawled quickly but does not guarantee indexing.

robotsTxt.question: What is a robots.txt file?
robotsTxt.answer: A robots.txt file is a plain text file placed at the root of your website (e.g., example.com/robots.txt) that tells search engine crawlers which pages or sections of your site they should or should not access. It follows the Robots Exclusion Protocol and is the first file crawlers check before scanning your site.

robotsTxt.question: What if my site does not have a robots.txt?
robotsTxt.answer: While a robots.txt file is not strictly required, having one is a best practice. Without it, search engines will attempt to crawl every accessible page on your site, which can waste crawl budget on unimportant pages and potentially expose staging or admin areas in search results.

robotsTxt.question: Does robots.txt hide pages from users?
robotsTxt.answer: No. The robots.txt file only provides instructions to web crawlers. It does not restrict human visitors from accessing pages. If someone has the direct URL, they can still visit a page that is blocked in robots.txt. For actual access control, use password protection or server-side authentication.

robotsTxt.question: What is crawl budget and why does it matter?
robotsTxt.answer: Crawl budget is the number of pages a search engine crawler will visit on your site within a given timeframe. A properly configured robots.txt helps prioritize your most important pages by blocking crawlers from low-value or duplicate content, ensuring your crawl budget is spent efficiently.

robotsTxt.question: Is robots.txt a security feature?
robotsTxt.answer: Not really. The robots.txt file itself is publicly accessible, so anyone can read it. It should not be used to hide sensitive data or confidential content. For security, rely on proper authentication, authorization, and "noindex" meta tags instead. Use robots.txt primarily for crawl management.

llmsTxt.question: Is llms.txt an official web standard?
llmsTxt.answer: No. llms.txt is a community proposal, not an official standard ratified by a body like the W3C, and major AI providers have not formally committed to reading it. It's an emerging convention. Adding one is low-risk and low-cost, but treat it as a helpful signal rather than a guaranteed ranking factor.

llmsTxt.question: Do search engines use llms.txt?
llmsTxt.answer: Traditional search engines like Google rely on robots.txt and sitemap.xml, not llms.txt, for crawling and indexing. llms.txt is aimed at AI models and AI search experiences. It doesn't replace your sitemap or robots.txt, it sits alongside them for a different audience.

llmsTxt.question: How often should I update it?
llmsTxt.answer: Refresh it whenever your important pages change, for example when you launch, rename, or retire key content. For most sites a quick review every few months is enough. The main thing to avoid is letting it point at dead or outdated URLs.

llmsTxt.question: Can I have multiple llms.txt files?
llmsTxt.answer: The primary file should live at your domain root (example.com/llms.txt). You generally want one canonical file per site so models have a single source of truth. Large or multi-section sites sometimes add supplementary files, but the root file is what matters most.

llmsTxt.question: What's the difference between llms.txt and llms-full.txt?
llmsTxt.answer: llms.txt is a concise index: titles, descriptions, and links to your key pages. llms-full.txt is a heavier variant that includes the full page content in markdown, so models can read your content directly without fetching each page. This generator produces the standard llms.txt.

seoCompetitorAnalysis.question: What is an SEO competitor analysis and why does it matter?
seoCompetitorAnalysis.answer: An SEO competitor analysis is the process of comparing your website's search engine performance against a competitor's across key metrics like organic traffic, keyword rankings, backlinks, and domain authority. It matters because understanding where competitors outperform you reveals actionable gaps - specific keywords they rank for that you don't, content strategies driving their traffic, and link-building opportunities you're missing. Without competitor analysis, you're optimizing blind.

seoCompetitorAnalysis.question: How does this free SEO competitor analysis tool work?
seoCompetitorAnalysis.answer: Enter your domain and a competitor's domain, and the tool pulls real-time SEO data for both. It compares organic traffic estimates, total ranking keywords, backlink profiles, and domain trust scores side by side. It then cross-references both keyword portfolios to show shared keywords, keywords unique to each domain, and ranking differences.

seoCompetitorAnalysis.question: What is keyword overlap and how should I use it?
seoCompetitorAnalysis.answer: Keyword overlap shows three things: keywords both domains rank for (shared), keywords only your competitor ranks for (unique to competitor), and keywords only you rank for (unique to you). Shared keywords reveal where you're directly competing - check if your positions are higher or lower. Keywords unique to your competitor are content gaps you should consider targeting. Keywords unique to you are your competitive advantages to protect and strengthen.

seoCompetitorAnalysis.question: How do I find keyword gaps between my site and a competitor?
seoCompetitorAnalysis.answer: Start by comparing both domains side by side. Export or review the keywords your competitor ranks for, compare them against the keywords your site ranks for, and focus on the missing terms where they appear on page one while you are much lower or absent. The best gaps are not always the biggest keywords. Prioritize searches where the current ranking pages look beatable: shallow content, weak topical coverage, outdated information, or a SERP without many high-authority domains. Those are the gaps where a focused page has a realistic chance to compete.

seoCompetitorAnalysis.question: How often should I run an SEO competitor analysis?
seoCompetitorAnalysis.answer: A good rhythm is a quarterly deep dive plus a lighter monthly check-in. SEO changes constantly: competitors publish new pages, rankings move, and search results shift after algorithm updates. Treat competitor analysis as an ongoing process, not a one-time report. A full quarterly review helps you spot larger strategy changes, while a monthly gap check catches new content and ranking movement early. The sooner you identify a gap, the easier it is to close before a competitor's page builds more authority.

seoCompetitorAnalysis.question: Can I use this tool to analyze competitors in any niche or country?
seoCompetitorAnalysis.answer: Yes, you can compare any two domains regardless of industry or niche. The analysis currently uses US search data by default, which covers the largest English-language search market. The tool is most valuable when comparing domains that compete for similar audiences or keywords - for example, two SaaS companies, two e-commerce stores in the same category, or two content publishers covering overlapping topics.

h1Checker.question: Should every page have an H1?
h1Checker.answer: Yes. Every indexable page should have exactly one H1 that describes its main topic. It helps both readers and search engines understand the page at a glance, and it is one of the simplest on-page SEO elements to get right.

h1Checker.question: Can a page have multiple H1 tags?
h1Checker.answer: HTML5 technically allows multiple H1s, but for SEO it is best to use just one. A single H1 gives search engines one clear main heading; multiple H1s can dilute that signal and make the page's focus ambiguous.

h1Checker.question: Does the H1 tag affect SEO rankings?
h1Checker.answer: The H1 is a meaningful on-page signal rather than a direct ranking factor on its own. A clear, keyword-relevant H1 helps search engines understand and match your page to queries, which supports rankings alongside content quality and other factors.

h1Checker.question: Should the H1 be the same as the title tag?
h1Checker.answer: They can overlap but should not be identical. Writing the H1 as a variant of the title tag lets you target additional related queries and gives you two chances to communicate relevance instead of one.

h1Checker.question: What is the ideal H1 length?
h1Checker.answer: Aim for roughly 20 to 70 characters. That range is long enough to be descriptive and keyword-rich, yet short enough to stay scannable and avoid being cut off in some layouts.

h1Checker.question: How is the H1 different from the title tag in HTML?
h1Checker.answer: The title tag lives in the document head as the <title> element and appears in the browser tab and search results. The H1 is an <h1> element in the page body and is the visible main heading readers see on the page itself.

h1Checker.question: Is this H1 checker really free?
h1Checker.answer: Yes, completely free with no sign-up required. Paste a draft H1 or check a live URL as many times as you like — there is no cost, login, or credit card.

llmsTxtValidator.question: Where do I put my llms.txt file?
llmsTxtValidator.answer: At the root of your domain, so it loads at https://yourdomain.com/llms.txt. It should sit alongside files like robots.txt, not in a subfolder. The URL mode of this validator looks for it there automatically.

llmsTxtValidator.question: Does a valid llms.txt guarantee I appear in AI answers?
llmsTxtValidator.answer: No. A valid file means the format is correct, nothing more. Whether models cite you depends on content quality, authority, and overall AI search visibility. llms.txt is a low-cost foundation, not a ranking guarantee.

llmsTxtValidator.question: How is llms.txt different from robots.txt?
llmsTxtValidator.answer: robots.txt tells crawlers what to avoid, it is about exclusion. llms.txt is opt-in and does the opposite: it invites models in and points them at the pages you most want understood and cited. They solve different problems and can coexist.

llmsTxtValidator.question: Is llms.txt required?
llmsTxtValidator.answer: No, it is entirely optional. Your site works fine without one. It is an emerging standard that may help AI tools understand your site, and because it is quick and free to add, many teams publish one to be future-ready.

llmsTxtValidator.question: What's the difference between llms.txt and llms-full.txt?
llmsTxtValidator.answer: llms.txt is a concise index: a title, a summary, and curated links. llms-full.txt is an optional companion that inlines the full text of those pages into one file, so a model can ingest your content without following every link. This tool validates the standard llms.txt format.

llmsTxtValidator.question: How often should I update it?
llmsTxtValidator.answer: Refresh it whenever your important pages change, for example after a redesign, a docs restructure, or a major launch. Otherwise a quarterly check is plenty. Re-run the validator after edits to catch broken links and formatting slips.

metaDescriptionChecker.question: What is the ideal meta description length in 2026?
metaDescriptionChecker.answer: Aim for roughly 120 to 160 characters. Mobile results show fewer characters than desktop, so staying near 120 keeps your snippet intact on phones while still using the available space on desktop.

metaDescriptionChecker.question: Does the meta description affect SEO rankings?
metaDescriptionChecker.answer: Not directly. It is not a ranking factor, but a compelling description improves click-through rate from the results page, and higher engagement can indirectly support your visibility over time.

metaDescriptionChecker.question: Why does Google sometimes ignore my meta description?
metaDescriptionChecker.answer: Google rewrites the snippet when it believes another passage on your page better matches the searcher's query. Writing a description that closely answers the target query reduces how often it overrides you.

metaDescriptionChecker.question: What's the difference between this checker and a SERP snippet preview?
metaDescriptionChecker.answer: This tool focuses on analyzing and validating your meta description with a live checklist and counters. A SERP snippet preview simulates the full search result, including the title tag and rich features.

metaDescriptionChecker.question: Can I check the meta description of any URL?
metaDescriptionChecker.answer: Yes. Switch to the From URL tab, paste a live page address, and click Fetch to pull its current meta description. The fetched text drops into the editor so you can analyze and improve it.

metaDescriptionChecker.question: How do I change a meta description on WordPress, Shopify, or Webflow?
metaDescriptionChecker.answer: On WordPress use an SEO plugin like Yoast or Rank Math; on Shopify edit the page's Search engine listing field; on Webflow set it in each page's SEO settings. All three let you paste a description directly.

metaDescriptionChecker.question: Is this meta description checker really free?

serpSnippetPreview.question: What is the ideal title tag length in 2026?
serpSnippetPreview.answer: Aim for 50–60 characters and under roughly 600 pixels on desktop. Google truncates by pixel width, not character count, so use the live preview to confirm your title renders in full before publishing.

serpSnippetPreview.question: What is the ideal meta description length?
serpSnippetPreview.answer: Around 150–160 characters, or under roughly 960 pixels on desktop. Mobile shows a little more. Keep it concise and benefit-driven so Google displays your wording instead of generating its own.

serpSnippetPreview.question: Why does Google sometimes rewrite my title tag?
serpSnippetPreview.answer: Google rewrites titles it considers too long, keyword-stuffed, vague, or a poor match for the query. Writing a clear, accurate, correctly sized title tag is the best way to keep your own wording in the results.

serpSnippetPreview.question: Does the meta description impact my Google rankings?
serpSnippetPreview.answer: Not directly. It is not a ranking factor, but it strongly influences click-through rate, and a higher CTR brings more traffic and positive engagement signals that support your rankings indirectly.

serpSnippetPreview.question: How is the mobile SERP different from desktop?
serpSnippetPreview.answer: Mobile results render as cards, use slightly different fonts, and allow different title and description lengths before truncation. This tool switches the preview and the character and pixel limits to match each device.

serpSnippetPreview.question: Can I preview my snippet with an AI Overview?
serpSnippetPreview.answer: Yes. Toggle the AI Overview feature to simulate Google's AI Overview block appearing above your result, which pushes your snippet down the page. On mobile it can drop well below the fold.

serpSnippetPreview.question: Why is my page snippet not showing in Google?
serpSnippetPreview.answer: The page may not be indexed yet, may be blocked by robots.txt or a noindex tag, or may be too new. Confirm it is crawlable and indexed, then give Google time to recrawl and show the updated snippet.

serpSnippetPreview.question: Is this SERP preview tool really free?

openGraphChecker.question: What is an Open Graph checker?
openGraphChecker.answer: An Open Graph checker fetches a page the way social platforms do, reads its og: and Twitter Card tags, and shows how the link will render when shared on Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Discord, WhatsApp and more. It flags missing or malformed tags and gives you a score so you can fix problems before you post.

openGraphChecker.question: Why are my OG tags not showing on Facebook?
openGraphChecker.answer: Facebook caches the first version of your tags it sees, so recent changes often will not appear until the cache refreshes. Confirm the tags are present in the page's raw HTML, then paste the URL into Facebook's Sharing Debugger and click Scrape Again to force a fresh crawl.

openGraphChecker.question: What is the difference between Open Graph and Twitter Cards?
openGraphChecker.answer: Open Graph (og:) is the shared standard most platforms read. Twitter Cards (twitter:) are X's own tags that override og: when present and fall back to it when absent. In practice you only need a few twitter: tags, such as twitter:card, and og: covers the rest.

openGraphChecker.question: How do I fix a missing og:image?
openGraphChecker.answer: Add an og:image tag pointing to an absolute URL (not a relative path) for an image that is at least 1200x630 pixels, under 8MB, and ideally under 500KB for WhatsApp. Use JPG, PNG or WebP, then re-check the URL and clear each platform's preview cache.

openGraphChecker.question: How do I clear the Facebook or LinkedIn preview cache?
openGraphChecker.answer: For Facebook, use the Sharing Debugger and click Scrape Again. For LinkedIn, use the Post Inspector and click Inspect to refresh the cached preview. Both force the platform to re-crawl your page and pick up your updated tags.

openGraphChecker.question: Does Open Graph affect SEO?
openGraphChecker.answer: Not directly. Open Graph tags are not a Google ranking factor, but they drive social click-through, which brings real referral traffic, and they give AI crawlers clean, structured context about your page. They are table stakes for a professional presence, not a ranking lever on their own.

robotsTxtGenerator.question: Does robots.txt affect SEO?
robotsTxtGenerator.answer: Indirectly, yes. It doesn't change rankings on its own, but it controls which pages crawlers can reach. Block the wrong path and important pages never get crawled; guide bots well and you protect your crawl budget for the pages that matter.

robotsTxtGenerator.question: Can I block Google from crawling my site?
robotsTxtGenerator.answer: Yes. Set Googlebot to Block, or use Disallow: / for all bots, and Google stops crawling. Note this won't remove pages that are already indexed, for that you need a noindex tag or a removal request in Search Console.

robotsTxtGenerator.question: What happens if I don't have a robots.txt file?
robotsTxtGenerator.answer: Crawlers assume they can access everything. That's fine for many small sites, but you lose the chance to steer crawl budget, keep bots out of private areas, and declare your sitemap in one place.

robotsTxtGenerator.question: Is robots.txt the same as noindex?
robotsTxtGenerator.answer: No. robots.txt controls crawling; noindex controls indexing. A page blocked in robots.txt can still appear in search if other sites link to it, because Google never crawls it to see a noindex tag. Use noindex to actually remove a page from results.

robotsTxtGenerator.question: Where do I upload my robots.txt file?
robotsTxtGenerator.answer: At the root of your domain, so it resolves at https://yourdomain.com/robots.txt. It will not work in a subfolder. Most hosts and CMSs let you add it through the file manager or an SEO plugin.

robotsTxtGenerator.question: Is this robots.txt generator really free?
robotsTxtGenerator.answer: Yes, completely free with no sign-up. Build, copy and download as many robots.txt files as you like. There is no login or credit card.

aiReadabilityChecker.question: What is an AI readability score?
aiReadabilityChecker.answer: It is a single number from 0 to 100 that estimates how easily AI engines can read, understand and cite your page. It combines five checks: answer-first content, structure, machine-readability, trust signals and crawler access.

aiReadabilityChecker.question: Is AI readability the same as SEO?
aiReadabilityChecker.answer: No. SEO is about ranking in traditional search. AI readability is about whether AI engines can quote and attribute your page. They overlap, but a page can rank well and still be hard for AI to cite.

aiReadabilityChecker.question: Will making my content AI-ready help me rank on Google too?
aiReadabilityChecker.answer: Usually yes. Clear answers, clean structure, schema and trust signals are good for both AI engines and Google. AI readability is a strong foundation for overall search performance.

aiReadabilityChecker.question: Do I need structured data to be cited by AI?
aiReadabilityChecker.answer: It helps a lot but is not strictly required. Schema like Article, FAQ or HowTo makes your content easier to parse and trust. Clear answers and structure matter even more.

aiReadabilityChecker.question: Can I check any URL, or only my own?
aiReadabilityChecker.answer: You can check any public URL. The page must be reachable, not behind a login and not blocked from crawlers. Private and localhost URLs are not supported.

aiReadabilityChecker.question: What's the difference between this and an AI visibility checker?
aiReadabilityChecker.answer: This checks whether a page is structured so AI can read and cite it, the on-page prerequisite. A visibility checker tests whether you are actually being cited. Citable first, cited second.

aiReadabilityChecker.question: Is this AI readability checker really free?
aiReadabilityChecker.answer: Yes. It is completely free with no sign-up. Paste a draft or scan a live URL and get your score and fixes instantly.

checklist.description: We're doing this in the background. Your full dashboard unlocks when it's done.

items.label: Discovering high-value keywords in your niche
items.detail: We analyze search trends, question patterns, and AI-generated answer topics to find the exact keywords your audience uses, including long-tail queries that drive qualified traffic.

items.label: Scanning your pages and learning your brand
items.detail: We crawl every page on your site to understand your products, services, writing style, and brand voice so every piece of content we create feels native to your brand.

items.label: Analyzing your LLM and AI search visibility
items.detail: We check how your website appears in AI-generated answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, and other LLMs to pinpoint where you're visible and where competitors are winning.

items.label: Auditing your site for AI visibility blockers
items.detail: We scan for technical issues like missing structured data, crawl restrictions, thin content signals, and schema gaps that could prevent search engines and LLMs from surfacing your pages.

items.label: Finding backlink exchange partners
items.detail: We search our network for high-quality, relevant websites in your niche to set up backlink exchanges that boost your domain authority and improve rankings across both traditional and AI search.

items.label: Mapping social and community opportunities
items.detail: We identify Reddit threads, Quora questions, and other community discussions that LLMs reference in their answers so you get ready-made opportunities to boost your AI visibility.

items.label: Building your personalized 30-day content plan
items.detail: Based on everything we've learned, we create a tailored content calendar with the right topics, article types, and publishing schedule to maximize your AEO and SEO impact from day one.

modal.heroDescription: Share your honest experience on G2 and we'll reward you
modal.tipsHeading: How to get your review approved
modal.tip1: No time to type? Record it. Choose G2's video option and just talk. G2 turns what you say into a written review, and your video is not published.
modal.tip2: Sign in with LinkedIn or your work email. It's the fastest way for G2 to verify you.
modal.tip3: Upload a screenshot of your BabyLoveGrowth dashboard when G2 asks. You get the "Current User" badge, and the screenshot is never made public.
modal.tip4: Be specific: what you use us for, which features you rely on (articles, backlinks, site audit, AI tracking) and what changed: traffic, rankings, domain rating, time saved.
modal.tip5: Mention what could be better too. Balanced reviews are more credible and get approved more easily.
modal.tip6: It takes about 10 minutes, less if you record it.
modal.check1: Use your own words. G2 rejects copied or templated text.
modal.check2: Any rating is fine. The $50 credit is for an honest review, positive or negative.
modal.check3: Base it on your own use of BabyLoveGrowth.
modal.check4: Once G2 approves it, email {email} with the name shown on your review. Your $50 credit will be applied to your next invoice within 24–48 hours.

improvements.title: Improved Articles
improvements.subtitle: Below you can find articles which need to be improved to start ranking better on Google and AI search.
improvements.explainer: We continuously review how the articles on your website perform in Google Search. When the data shows a clear opportunity to rank better, we rewrite that article, changing only the parts that need it.

scan.title: Scan performance
scan.description: Through Google Search Console, we track clicks, impressions, click-through rate and rankings for every article on your website.

rewrite.title: Rewrite with purpose
rewrite.description: On each improvement day, we rewrite the article with the clearest opportunity. We prepare it the day before, so it's ready for review on the day itself.

review.title: You stay in control
review.description: Approve or reject each change one by one. Nothing goes live until you approve, unless auto-approve is on. Safety-flagged rewrites always wait for your review.

howItWorks.eligibility: Articles that already perform well are left alone. To qualify, a page needs at least 90 days in Google Search and real search demand. Pages improved in the last 6 months, or rejected in the last 4 weeks, are skipped. When several pages qualify, the one with the most impressions goes first.

measure.title: Measure the impact
measure.description: About two weeks after an improvement goes live, we compare its clicks and impressions with the period before, so you can see what changed.

howItWorks.changesScope: We only change what the opportunity calls for. An article with a weak click-through rate gets a new title and description, while an outdated one gets its facts refreshed without new sections being added.

emptyState.title: Scanning for opportunities
emptyState.description: We're watching how your published articles perform in Google Search. The moment a page is worth improving, it'll show up here.

opportunityTooltips.STALE_CONTENT: The article hasn't been updated in over a year. Refreshing facts and figures keeps it competitive.

problemDetails.robots_txt_missing: We couldn't find /robots.txt. This small file tells search engines which pages they may read.
problemDetails.robots_txt_incorrect: Your robots.txt stops Google or Bing from reading your homepage, so it can't show in results.
problemDetails.sitemap_missing: We couldn't find a sitemap. It lists your pages so search engines find new ones quickly.
problemDetails.sitemap_incorrect: Your sitemap isn't valid XML, often because of a blank first line or a hidden character, so search engines may skip it.
problemDetails.llm_txt_missing: There is no /llms.txt. This file gives AI assistants a short guide to your most important pages.
problemDetails.ssl_missing: Your site doesn't load securely. Browsers warn visitors and search engines rank it lower.
problemDetails.meta_title_missing: The page has no title. Google shows the title as the clickable link in results.
problemDetails.meta_title_length: Aim for 45–60 characters. Longer titles get cut off in Google and shorter ones say too little.
problemDetails.meta_title_duplicates: The page has two or more title tags, so search engines may pick the wrong one.
problemDetails.meta_title_uniqueness: Several pages share this title, so search engines can't tell them apart.
problemDetails.meta_title_irrelevant: The title doesn't describe what's on the page, which costs clicks and rankings.
problemDetails.meta_description_missing: Without one, Google picks random text from the page to show under your link.
problemDetails.meta_description_length: Aim for 150–160 characters so the whole text shows under your link in Google.
problemDetails.meta_description_duplicates: The page has two or more description tags, so search engines may show the wrong one.
problemDetails.meta_description_uniqueness: Several pages share this description, so they look the same in search results.
problemDetails.meta_description_irrelevant: The description doesn't sum up the page, so fewer people click.
problemDetails.h1_missing: Each page needs one H1 that says what it's about. It helps search engines and screen readers.
problemDetails.h1_multiple: Use exactly one H1 per page so the main topic is clear.
problemDetails.canonical_missing: A canonical tag tells search engines which address is the main one, so copies don't compete.
problemDetails.canonical_duplicates: Two or more canonical tags confuse search engines. Keep one.
problemDetails.canonical_incorrect: The page says its main version lives on a different domain, so this page may not rank.
problemDetails.broken_link: A link on the page leads to an error, so visitors and crawlers hit a dead end.
problemDetails.page_speed_low: Google PageSpeed scores the page below 80 on desktop. Slow pages lose visitors and rankings.
problemDetails.image_large: Images over 100 KB slow the page down. Compress them or save them as WebP.
problemDetails.image_missing_alt_text: Alt text describes an image for screen readers and search engines.
problemDetails.image_poor_alt_text: The alt text is a file name, a generic word, or too short or long to describe the image.
problemDetails.image_broken: An image doesn't load, so visitors see an empty space.
problemDetails.image_unknown_format: We couldn't tell what kind of image this is, so some browsers may not show it.
problemDetails.json_ld_missing: Structured data (JSON-LD) tells Google and AI assistants what the page is, like a product, an article or a business.
problemDetails.json_ld_incorrect: The page has structured data, but it's incomplete or doesn't match the page.
problemDetails.missing_content_gaps: People ask questions about your topic that this page doesn't answer. AI assistants quote pages that do.

robots_txt_missing.title: Missing robots.txt file
robots_txt_missing.description: robots.txt is the first file crawlers look for. Without it, Google and AI crawlers can't find your sitemap through it, and you have no way to tell them what to skip.
robots_txt_missing.action: Add a robots.txt file at yoursite.com/robots.txt that allows crawling and includes a Sitemap line with your sitemap URL.

robots_txt_incorrect.title: Incorrect robots.txt configuration
robots_txt_incorrect.description: Your robots.txt blocks search engine crawlers such as Googlebot or Bingbot from your homepage, so your site can drop out of Google, Bing and the AI answers built on them.
robots_txt_incorrect.action: Remove the rule that blocks the crawlers listed in this issue, for example Disallow: / under User-agent: *.

sitemap_missing.title: Missing sitemap
sitemap_missing.description: A sitemap lists the pages you want found. Without one, Google and AI crawlers rely on links alone and can miss new or deeper pages.
sitemap_missing.action: Publish an XML sitemap at yoursite.com/sitemap.xml that lists your important pages, add it to robots.txt and submit it in Google Search Console.

sitemap_incorrect.title: Incorrect sitemap XML
sitemap_incorrect.description: Your sitemap has blank lines, hidden characters or broken XML, so search engines may not be able to read it at all.
sitemap_incorrect.action: Remove blank lines and hidden characters so the XML declaration is on the very first line, then check the file with a sitemap validator.

llm_txt_missing.title: Missing llms.txt file
llm_txt_missing.description: llms.txt is an emerging standard: a short, plain-text guide to your business and key pages, written for AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude. We couldn't find a valid one on your site.
llm_txt_missing.action: Add a plain-text llms.txt file at yoursite.com/llms.txt with a one-paragraph summary of your business and links to your most important pages.

json_ld_missing.title: Missing JSON-LD schema
json_ld_missing.description: Structured data (JSON-LD) tells search engines exactly what a page is, such as an article, a product or a business, and helps AI assistants understand it. Without it, the page can't get rich results such as review stars or prices.
json_ld_missing.action: Add JSON-LD that fits the page, for example Article for blog posts, Product for product pages, or Organization or LocalBusiness for your homepage.

json_ld_incorrect.title: Incorrect JSON-LD schema
json_ld_incorrect.description: This page has structured data, but it leaves out details that describe the page, so Google and AI assistants get an incomplete picture.
json_ld_incorrect.action: Update the JSON-LD with the suggested schema in this issue, then check it with Google's Rich Results Test.

meta_title_length.title: Meta title length issue
meta_title_length.description: Google cuts off titles longer than about 60 characters, and very short titles say too little. The title is what people read before deciding to click.
meta_title_length.action: Rewrite the title to 45–60 characters, with the most important words first.

meta_title_duplicates.title: Duplicate meta title tags
meta_title_duplicates.description: This page has more than one title tag, so search engines have to guess which one to show.
meta_title_duplicates.action: Remove the extra title tags so the page has one. Duplicates usually come from a theme and an SEO plugin both adding a title.

meta_title_uniqueness.title: Title duplicated across multiple pages
meta_title_uniqueness.description: When several pages share a title, Google can't tell them apart and they end up competing for the same searches.
meta_title_uniqueness.action: Give each page its own title that says what makes that page different.

meta_title_missing.title: Missing meta title
meta_title_missing.description: Without a title, Google makes one up from the page content, and it's usually less clear and less clickable than one you'd write.
meta_title_missing.action: Add a title of 45–60 characters that says what the page is about, with the most important words first.

meta_title_irrelevant.title: Irrelevant meta title
meta_title_irrelevant.description: The title doesn't match what the page is about, so Google may replace it in results and visitors who click don't find what they expected.
meta_title_irrelevant.action: Rewrite the title to describe what the page actually covers, using the words people search for.

meta_description_length.title: Meta description length
meta_description_length.description: Google cuts off descriptions longer than about 160 characters, and very short ones don't give people a reason to click.
meta_description_length.action: Rewrite the description to 110–160 characters, with the key point first.

meta_description_missing.title: Missing meta description
meta_description_missing.description: Without a meta description, Google picks a snippet from the page itself, which is often less convincing than a summary you write.
meta_description_missing.action: Add a meta description of 110–160 characters that summarizes the page and gives people a reason to click.

meta_description_duplicates.title: Duplicate meta description tags
meta_description_duplicates.description: This page has more than one meta description tag, so search engines have to guess which one to show.
meta_description_duplicates.action: Remove the extra meta description tags so the page has one. Duplicates usually come from a theme and an SEO plugin both adding one.

meta_description_uniqueness.title: Not unique meta description
meta_description_uniqueness.description: When several pages share a description, they look the same in search results and people can't tell which one to click.
meta_description_uniqueness.action: Write a description for each page that sums up what that specific page offers.

meta_description_irrelevant.title: Irrelevant meta description
meta_description_irrelevant.description: The description doesn't match what the page is about, so Google often replaces it with its own snippet and visitors may not find what they expected.
meta_description_irrelevant.action: Rewrite the description to summarize what the page actually covers, using the words people search for.

page_speed_low.title: Low page speed
page_speed_low.description: This page scores below 80 in Google PageSpeed Insights. Slow pages lose visitors, especially on mobile, and page experience is one of the signals Google uses to rank pages.
page_speed_low.action: Work through the suggestions in the PageSpeed report, usually compressing images, removing unused scripts and turning on caching. Aim for 80 or higher.

h1_missing.title: Missing H1 tag
h1_missing.description: The H1 is the main heading of a page. Without one, readers, screen readers and AI assistants lose a clear signal of what the page is about.
h1_missing.action: Add one H1 at the top of the page that states its main topic.

h1_multiple.title: Multiple H1 tags
h1_multiple.description: With more than one H1 there's no single main heading, so it's less clear to readers, screen readers and AI assistants what the page is mainly about.
h1_multiple.action: Keep one H1 for the main topic and change the others to H2 or H3 subheadings.

canonical_missing.title: Missing canonical URL
canonical_missing.description: A canonical tag tells search engines which URL is the main version of a page. Without it, Google chooses one itself and may pick a copy, such as a URL with tracking parameters.
canonical_missing.action: Add a canonical tag that points to this page's own URL.

canonical_duplicates.title: Multiple canonical URLs
canonical_duplicates.description: This page has more than one canonical tag, so search engines can't tell which URL is the main one and may ignore them all.
canonical_duplicates.action: Remove the extra canonical tags so one remains. Duplicates usually come from a theme and an SEO plugin both adding one.

canonical_incorrect.title: Incorrect canonical URL
canonical_incorrect.description: The canonical tag points to another website, which tells search engines to show that site's page instead of yours.
canonical_incorrect.action: Change the canonical tag to a URL on your own domain, usually this page's own URL.

image_large.title: Large image
image_large.description: Images over 150 KB are often the main reason pages load slowly, especially on mobile, and slow pages lose visitors.
image_large.action: Resize the image to the size it's shown at and compress it below 150 KB. Saving it as WebP usually makes it much smaller.

image_poor_alt_text.title: Poor image alt text
image_poor_alt_text.description: This image's alt text doesn't describe what it shows, so screen reader users, search engines and AI assistants can't tell what's in it.
image_poor_alt_text.action: Rewrite the alt text as a short, specific description of what the image shows.

too_short.title: Image alt text too short
too_short.description: The image has alt text, but it is under 5 characters — too short to describe the image for accessibility and image SEO.
too_short.action: Expand the alt text into a short description of the image (at least 5 characters)

too_long.title: Image alt text too long
too_long.description: The alt text is over 160 characters. Screen reader users have to listen to all of it, and longer details belong in a caption or the page text.
too_long.action: Shorten the alt text to 160 characters or fewer while keeping it descriptive

generic.title: Generic image alt text
generic.description: The image's alt text is a generic word like "image" or "logo" that does not describe what the image shows.
generic.action: Replace the generic alt text with a short description of what the image shows

filename.title: Image alt text is a filename
filename.description: The alt text is a file name, so it tells screen readers, search engines and AI assistants nothing about what the image shows.
filename.action: Replace the filename with a short description of what the image shows

image_missing_alt_text.title: Missing alt text
image_missing_alt_text.description: Alt text tells screen readers, search engines and AI assistants what an image shows. Without it, screen reader users miss the image and it's less likely to appear in image search.
image_missing_alt_text.action: Add alt text that describes what the image shows in a short phrase.

image_broken.title: Broken image
image_broken.description: This image doesn't load, so visitors see a broken placeholder and the image can't appear in image search.
image_broken.action: Fix the image URL or upload the image again, or remove it if you no longer need it.

image_unknown_format.title: Unknown image format
image_unknown_format.description: We couldn't tell what type of image this is, which usually means the server sends it with the wrong file type, so some browsers may not show it.
image_unknown_format.action: Save the image as JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or SVG and make sure your server sends the matching file type.

ssl_missing.title: Missing SSL certificate
ssl_missing.description: Your site has no working SSL certificate (it's missing, expired or invalid), so browsers warn visitors that it's not secure, and Google prefers secure sites in its rankings.
ssl_missing.action: Install or renew the SSL certificate (most hosts include a free one) and redirect every HTTP address to HTTPS.

broken_link.title: Broken link
broken_link.description: This link leads to a page that doesn't work, so visitors who click it hit a dead end.
broken_link.action: Update the link to the right URL, point it to a working page on the same topic, or remove it.

missing_content_gaps.title: Missing content gaps
missing_content_gaps.description: This page doesn't cover topics your potential customers search for in Google and ask AI assistants about, so you miss those visitors.
missing_content_gaps.action: Add sections that answer the missing topics and questions listed for this page, or create new pages for them.

duda.rssFeedDescription: Use this RSS feed in Duda to import your latest articles.

prerequisites.title: Before you start
prerequisites.description: Duda doesn't connect directly, it uses an <bold>RSS feed to pull your articles</bold> automatically.
prerequisites.checkSite: I have a <bold>Duda site</bold> I can edit and publish
prerequisites.checkArticle: I've <bold>published at least one article</bold> (the RSS feed needs content to pull)
prerequisites.noArticleBody: No problem — you can set this up now. The feed will be empty until your first article publishes, then Duda fills it in automatically. You can generate and publish one from your Content Plan.

feed.title: Generate your RSS feed URL
feed.description: Duda pulls your articles from an <bold>RSS feed</bold>. Generate the URL below, then add it to your Duda site — that's the whole setup.
feed.copyNote: <bold>Copy this URL</bold> — you'll paste it into Duda in the next step.
feed.hint: Tip: change <bold>limit=10</bold> in the URL to control <bold>how many articles</bold> Duda shows.
feed.generateHint: Generate your RSS feed URL. It's unique to your site and already includes everything Duda needs — there's no separate key to manage.
feed.regenerateNote: Regenerating creates a new URL and disables the old one — if you've already added it to Duda, update it there with the new URL.

addFeed.title: Add the RSS feed to Duda
addFeed.description: Add Duda's built-in <bold>RSS Feed</bold> widget to the page where you want your articles, then paste your feed URL.
addFeed.intro: Do this in the Duda editor. Open your site from your Duda dashboard:
addFeed.step1: Open your site in the <bold>Duda Website Editor</bold>.
addFeed.step2: In the left sidebar, click <bold>Add → Elements</bold>, search <bold>“RSS Feed”</bold>, and <bold>drag</bold> the widget onto the page where you want your articles.
addFeed.step3: The <bold>RSS Feed Content</bold> panel usually opens automatically when you drop the widget. If it doesn't, right-click the widget and select <bold>Edit Content</bold> (in Flex mode and Editor 2.0, use the widget's floating <bold>Edit Content</bold> button).
addFeed.step4: <bold>Paste the RSS feed URL</bold> you copied into the field, adjust the display settings (number of posts, layout), then click <bold>Publish</bold>.
addFeed.displayNote: The RSS Feed widget <bold>displays</bold> your articles on this page, it doesn't add them to Duda's native Blog. Want real blog posts instead? The next step imports the same feed into your Duda Blog.
addFeed.helpLink: Stuck? See Duda's RSS Feed widget guide
addFeed.mediaAlt: Adding and configuring the RSS Feed widget in the Duda editor

blogImport.title: Import your articles into Duda's Blog
blogImport.description: Duda's native <bold>Blog</bold> can import the same feed, turning your articles into real blog posts on your site.
blogImport.intro: Do this in the Duda editor, on the site where you want the posts:
blogImport.step1: Open your site in the <bold>Duda Website Editor</bold>.
blogImport.step2: In the left sidebar, click <bold>Blog</bold>, then open the <bold>Import</bold> tab.
blogImport.step3: <bold>Paste the RSS feed URL</bold> you copied into the <bold>Enter RSS feed URL</bold> field.
blogImport.step4: Click <bold>Import Posts</bold>, then <bold>Publish</bold> your site so the posts go live.
blogImport.mediaAlt: Importing an RSS feed from the Blog panel in the Duda editor

connected.title: You're all set
connected.description: Duda pulls your articles from the RSS feed you added, new articles appear automatically.
connected.verify1: Publish your Duda site if you haven't already
connected.verify2: Open your live site and go to the page with the RSS Feed widget, or to your Blog if you imported the posts
connected.verify3: Confirm your BabyLoveGrowth articles appear (it can take Duda a few minutes to pull the feed the first time)
connected.note: Duda syncs from the RSS feed, so make sure <bold>at least one article is published</bold> for it to show content.

step1.title: Before you start
step1.description: The Wix integration requires an existing blog with <bold>at least one published post.</bold> If no blog is detected, the connection will fail with a "No blog instance found" error.
step1.howToAddBlog: How to add a blog in Wix
step1.checkBlog: The <bold>Wix Blog</bold> app is added to my site
step1.checkOwner: I can sign in as the site's <bold>account owner</bold> — API keys created by co-owners or collaborators are rejected by Wix

step2.title: Find your Site ID
step2.description: Open your Wix dashboard and look at the URL in your <bold>browser address bar.</bold>
step2.mediaAlt: Finding the Site ID in the Wix dashboard URL

step3.title: Create your API key
step3.description: Generate the key and set its permissions — everything happens on one Wix screen.
step3.intro: The button below takes you straight to your Wix API Keys page. You may be asked to sign in.
step3.step3: Under <bold>Permissions</bold>, expand <bold>All site permissions</bold> and turn on both of these:
step3.siteAccessNote: If Wix asks which sites the key can access, pick <bold>All sites</bold> — or make sure your site is included. A key limited to other sites is rejected with a 403 error.
step3.mediaAlt: Generating an API key in Wix Account Settings

step4.title: Verify your email & copy the key
step4.description: To finish creating the key, Wix asks you to <bold>verify your identity</bold>.
step4.step1: Click <bold>Generate Key</bold> — Wix sends a verification code to your email
step4.step2: Enter the code and click <bold>Verify & Generate Key</bold>
step4.step3: <bold>Copy the key</bold> that appears — you'll paste it in the next step
step4.keyFormatHint: Wix keys are long, span <bold>several lines</bold>, and start with <bold>IST.</bold> — that's normal. Copy the whole thing.
step4.important: <bold>Important:</bold> <subtle>Wix only shows this key</subtle> <bold>once</bold>. <subtle>Copy it before leaving the page.</subtle>

step5.title: Paste your key & connect
step5.description: Paste the API key and choose how articles should be posted. We verify the key with Wix before saving.
step5.noBlogFieldError: Your key works, but no blog was found on this Wix site.
step5.noBlogTitle: Your Wix site doesn't have a blog yet
step5.noBlogBody: Your key and Site ID are fine — but the site has no <bold>Wix Blog</bold> app, so there's nothing to publish into. Add it (it's free), then click Connect again.
step5.permissionHintTitle: Wix rejected the key. The three most common causes:
step5.permissionHint1: 1. The key is missing the <bold>Wix Blog</bold> permission — check its permission list.
step5.permissionHint2: 2. The key was created by a <bold>co-owner or collaborator</bold> — it must come from the site owner's account.
step5.permissionHint3: 3. The key's <bold>site access</bold> is limited to specific sites that don't include this one.

connected.title: Wix connected!
connected.description: Your site is linked. Verify it's working by publishing a test article.
connected.label: Wix site
connected.step3: In Wix, go to your site dashboard → Blog
connected.step4: You'll see the article appear there.

step6.reviewNoticeBody: That's expected. Shopify shows this notice for any app you create yourself instead of installing from the Shopify App Store — it only means Shopify hasn't reviewed it, not that anything is wrong. This is your own private app, with permission limited to reading and publishing blog content. It's safe to click Install, and publishing works exactly as expected.

prerequisites.checkApp: I have a <bold>Next.js (App Router)</bold> project I can edit and deploy

step1.title: Install the package
step1.description: Add the official BabyLoveGrowth read client to your Next.js App Router project.
step1.callout: <bold>This is a developer integration.</bold> <subtle>You install an npm package and copy a starter blog folder into your Next.js (App Router) project.</subtle>

step2.title: Add your API key
step2.description: Create a .env.local file in your project and add this single server-side variable.
step2.apiKeyPlaceholder: No API key yet — click Generate.
step2.important: <bold>Important:</bold> <subtle>Keep this key server-side only. Never expose it with a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix or in client components.</subtle>

step3.title: Configure next.config
step3.description: Allow remote article images so Next.js can optimize them.
step3.hint: Add the <bold>images</bold> key inside your existing Next.js config object. Replace <bold>*</bold> with your specific image host for tighter security.

step4.title: Scaffold the blog & run
step4.description: Add the blog to your app, then start your site:
step4.step1: Run <bold>npm run dev</bold> and open <bold>/blog</bold> to see your articles.
step4.step2: Prefer manual setup? Copy the starter <bold>app/blog</bold> folder into your project instead.

connected.title: Next.js Blog connected!
connected.description: Your API key is ready. Use it in your Next.js project to render your blog.
connected.label: Next.js Blog
connected.remember: <bold>Remember:</bold> <subtle>Keep your API key server-side only. Your site uses daily ISR caching, so new articles can take up to a day to appear unless you redeploy.</subtle>

faqs.question: Which AI models do you track?
faqs.answer: ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude, each scored separately. That matters because a brand is often named by one model and missed entirely by another.

faqs.question: How many prompts can I track?
faqs.answer: The visibility score is measured across a tracked set of prompts, 25 on the standard plan. You can change which ones are in the set at any time from Manage prompts.

faqs.question: How often do you refresh the data?
faqs.answer: Weekly. Every tracked prompt is run again across the models, so the score, the competitor ranking and the sentiment reading all stay current.

faqs.question: Where do the prompts come from and can I add my own?
faqs.answer: We generate them from your category and the questions buyers actually ask, grouped by intent from awareness through to buying. You can edit that set and add your own.

faqs.question: What does the visibility score mean?
faqs.answer: The share of tracked answers where your brand appears. A score of 67% means you were named in roughly two out of every three responses across the prompts and models being tracked.

faqs.question: How do you measure sentiment?
faqs.answer: We read how the models describe you, not just whether they name you, and score it from 0 to 100. Below 25 reads as negative, 25 to 75 as neutral and above 75 as positive.

faqs.question: Can I track my competitors too?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you do not have to name them first. We pick up the brands AI mentions alongside you, rank them by visibility and show the gap between you and the leader.

faqs.question: Why does being mentioned by AI matter for my revenue?
faqs.answer: Visitors arriving from an AI answer convert better than any other channel. Adobe measured 42% higher conversion and 37% more revenue per visit, and Semrush put the average gap at 4.4x across industries.

faqs.question: Why does commenting on Reddit help me show up in AI answers?
faqs.answer: Reddit is one of the two most-cited domains across ChatGPT, Google AI Mode and Perplexity. When a model answers a question about your category it often reads a Reddit thread first, so a brand named in that thread can end up in the answer.

faqs.question: Why don't you post the comments automatically?
faqs.answer: Reddit detects and bans automated accounts, a ban takes the whole account history with it, and a link posted by a bot earns no citation at all because the thread gets removed. You post it yourself, it takes thirty seconds, and the account survives.

faqs.question: Do you post on Reddit for me?
faqs.answer: No. We find the thread and write the comment, then you review it and post it from your own account. That is what keeps the participation genuine and the account safe.

faqs.question: Will I get banned for self-promotion?
faqs.answer: Not if the comment reads like a person answering the question. We write responses that address what was actually asked and mention the brand only where it is relevant, and you review every one before it goes out.

faqs.question: Which subreddits and topics do you watch?
faqs.answer: The ones tied to the keywords you choose. You set the topics that matter to the brand and we scan Reddit and Quora continuously, so the subreddits follow from your keywords rather than a fixed list.

faqs.question: How many opportunities do I get each week?
faqs.answer: It depends on how much your topics are being discussed. We surface every relevant thread we find rather than filling a quota, and you decide which ones are worth answering.

faqs.question: Can I edit the comment before posting it?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every suggested comment can be edited, so you can rewrite as much or as little as you like before copying it across to the thread.

faqs.question: Do I need a Reddit account with existing karma?
faqs.answer: An account with some history behind it gets more traction and is less likely to be filtered, so an existing personal or brand account works better than one created for this. Either way the posting stays with you.

faqs.question: What difference does this make to my traffic?
faqs.answer: Two of the eleven checks have published numbers behind them. On page speed, Deloitte studied 30 million sessions across 37 brands and found that cutting 0.1 second off mobile load time raised conversions by 8.4% in retail and 10.1% in travel, with average order value up 9.2%. faqs.question: What is a backlink and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: A backlink is a link from another website to yours. Search engines and AI models read them as votes of confidence, so the more relevant sites link to you, the higher your own pages rank.

faqs.question: What do you check?
faqs.answer: Eleven checks on every page we can reach: page speed, meta title, meta description, canonical URL, broken links, image optimization, sitemap, robots.txt, SSL, llms.txt and JSON-LD schema. The last two are what most audit tools skip, and they are what AI crawlers rely on.

faqs.question: How often do you rescan my site?
faqs.answer: Every week, automatically. Scores and newly discovered issues stay current without you starting a scan, and you can watch the health score move over time.

faqs.question: Do you correct the issues or just report them?
faqs.answer: Every issue comes with a plain explanation of what is wrong and step by step instructions to fix it, plus a copy-ready prompt you can hand to an AI assistant. Applying the change happens on your side, and a recheck confirms it worked.

faqs.question: What is llms.txt and do I need one?
faqs.answer: It is a small file that tells AI models what your site is about and which pages matter. Traditional audits ignore it. We check whether you have one and flag it if you do not.

faqs.question: Does this work on Wix, Shopify and Webflow?
faqs.answer: Yes. We scan your live pages, so the platform behind them makes no difference. You apply the fixes wherever you manage your content.

faqs.question: Can I choose which pages get checked?
faqs.answer: We scan the whole site by default so nothing important is missed, and results break down page by page with a score and issue count for each. Get in touch if you need a narrower scope.

faqs.question: Do I need a developer to apply the changes?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most fixes are meta titles, descriptions and headings you can edit in your CMS. A few, like adding llms.txt or JSON-LD schema, may need someone with access to your site's code, and the instructions say exactly what to change.

faqs.question: What is a backlink and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: A backlink is a link from another website to yours. Search engines and AI models read them as votes of confidence, so the more relevant sites link to you, the higher your own pages rank.

faqs.question: Is exchanging backlinks safe for SEO?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as the sites are real and the links are contextual. Every website is vetted for quality and traffic before it joins, and adult, illegal, gray-hat and PBN sites are rejected.

faqs.question: How does the credit system work?
faqs.answer: Every account starts with 100 credits so you can receive backlinks straight away. You earn more credits whenever one of your articles gives a link to a partner site, and you spend them when you receive a link. Unused credits roll over.

faqs.question: How long before my domain rating moves?
faqs.answer: It builds gradually as links accumulate, so expect a few months rather than a few weeks. Samwell.ai saw their domain rating climb over four months in the network.

faqs.question: What sites will link to me?
faqs.answer: Real businesses from the 5,000+ sites in the network, matched to your niche. Only about a third of applicants pass vetting, and you can see the source site and its quality for every link you receive.

faqs.question: How many backlinks do I get each month?
faqs.answer: Usually 9 to 12 contextual links a month, included in the $99 plan. The exact number depends on your credit balance, and you can add bonus credits any time to go faster.

faqs.question: Where exactly is my link placed?
faqs.answer: Inside the body of a brand new article published by another business in the network, on a topic relevant to yours. No footers, sidebars or link pages.

faqs.question: Do I choose the anchor text?
faqs.answer: You pick the topics and pages you want to be associated with, and the anchor is written to read naturally in the sentence around it. Varied, natural anchors are what keeps a link profile safe.

faqs.question: What happens if a link gets removed?
faqs.answer: We keep crawling every placement, so your dashboard shows the live status of each link along with the source site and the date it went up. If one stops being live you will see it flagged there.

faqs.question: Do I keep the backlinks if I cancel?
faqs.answer: Yes. Links already placed live inside articles on other people's sites and are not pulled down when you leave. You simply stop receiving new placements.

faqs.question: Will Google penalize AI-written content?
faqs.answer: No. Google penalizes low-quality content, not content written with AI. Every article is researched against real search results, structured properly and sourced, which is the same bar Google applies to human writing.

faqs.question: Can AI-written blog posts actually rank on Google?
faqs.answer: Yes. Topics are chosen from real search demand in your niche and each article is built for how Google evaluates pages. Myhair.ai grew impressions by 855% and Operacinesistema grew traffic 600x this way.

faqs.question: Can I review or edit an article before it goes live?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every article lands in your dashboard where you can edit, approve or reject it. If you would rather not review anything, leave automatic publishing on and articles go live on your schedule.

faqs.question: Who picks the topics and can I suggest my own?
faqs.answer: We plan a month of topics from your business, your competitors and what people search before buying. You can add your own topics at any time and remove any you do not want written.

faqs.question: How do you learn my brand voice?
faqs.answer: We study your site, products and existing content, then apply your tone, terminology and internal links to every article. You can refine the voice whenever it drifts from how you would say it.

faqs.question: Do I keep the articles if I cancel?
faqs.answer: Yes. Anything already published to your site is yours to keep. Cancelling stops future articles, it never removes past ones.

faqs.question: What if my CMS is not on the list?
faqs.answer: We publish directly to WordPress, Webflow, Wix, Shopify, Framer, Ghost and Snapps. For anything else, including custom stacks, our API covers publishing.

faqs.question: What languages does the AI Blog Writer support?
faqs.answer: Over 50 languages, written natively rather than translated, so grammar and tone read like a local wrote them. If yours is missing, contact us and we will add it.

faqs.question: How fast can the AI Blog Writer create content?
faqs.answer: Your first article goes live around 15 minutes after you connect your site, then up to 30 articles publish each month without you doing anything.

faqs.question: Do I need writing experience to use the AI Blog Writer?
faqs.answer: No. Connect your site once and research, writing and publishing are handled for you. Reviewing drafts is optional, not required.

errors.tooMany: You can check up to {max} URLs at once. We checked the first {max}.
errors.generic: Couldn't check that URL. Please try again.

reasons.noindex: This page has a noindex tag, which tells Google to keep it out of the index.
reasons.http_error: The page returned an HTTP error, so Google can't crawl or index it.
reasons.generic: Google has no record of this URL yet. It may be new, blocked, or not linked well enough to be discovered.

result.tableHint: Full breakdown in the table below.

steps.title: Paste a URL
steps.description: Drop in any page — yours or a competitor's. Switch to multiple-URL mode to check up to 20 at once.

steps.title: Run the check
steps.description: We query Google for that exact URL and pull back what it has on file — no login, no Search Console.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.description: See if it's indexed, the title and snippet Google shows, and flags for title rewrites or canonical drift.

resultStates.description: A public check can't return Google's exact internal reason, so we map your result to the states you'll also see in Search Console.

items.title: Indexed
items.body: Google has this exact URL in its index and can show it in search results. You'll see the title and snippet it currently displays.

items.title: Not indexed
items.body: Google has no record of this URL, so it can't rank. Either it hasn't been crawled yet or something is blocking it — see the common reasons below.

items.title: Crawled, currently not indexed
items.body: Google visited the page but chose not to index it. This Search Console state usually signals thin, duplicate, or low-value content.

items.title: Discovered, not indexed
items.body: Google knows the URL exists but hasn't crawled it yet. This Search Console state often points to crawl-budget or internal-linking gaps.

items.title: Indexed under a different URL
items.body: Google indexed another version of the page — a canonical, trailing-slash, or parameter variant. The URL you checked isn't the one that ranks.

items.title: A noindex tag
items.description: A meta robots or X-Robots-Tag noindex tells Google to keep the page out of the index.

items.title: Blocked by robots.txt
items.description: If robots.txt disallows the path, Google can't crawl it and won't index it.

chapters.title: Indexing is the gate to every Google visit.
chapters.description: Two short reads on why indexing comes before everything else — and where it stops being enough.

items.title: Why indexing matters for SEO
items.kicker: No index, no rankings, no traffic.
items.body: Indexing is the step before ranking: Google can only show pages it has stored in its index. If a page isn't indexed it can't appear for any query, no matter how strong the content or how many links point to it. That's why indexing is the first thing to confirm when a page gets zero impressions — optimizing keywords or building links does nothing until the page is actually in the index.

items.title: Indexed in Google vs visible in AI search
items.kicker: Indexing is table stakes; getting cited is the next layer.
items.body: Being indexed gets you into Google's results, but AI answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google's AI Overviews pull from a different, narrower set of trusted sources. A page can be perfectly indexed and still never get cited by an AI engine. Generative engine optimization (GEO) is about earning those citations with clear structure, quotable answers, and authority signals AI models trust. Run a free GEO audit to see how your pages show up across AI search.
