whatIs.title: What is schema markup?
whatIs.sub1Title: Structured data and JSON-LD, explained simply
whatIs.sub1Body: Schema markup is a small block of code that describes your page to search engines in a vocabulary they fully understand — schema.org. JSON-LD is the format Google recommends: a tidy script you drop into your page that spells out what each thing on it is — an article, a product, a business, a FAQ. You write it once; visitors never see it.
whatIs.sub2Title: Where the markup sits on your page
whatIs.sub2Body: The JSON-LD lives in a script tag of type application/ld+json, usually inside the head of your HTML. It sits alongside your content, not inside it, so it never changes how the page looks. Search engines and AI crawlers read it to label your content with confidence.

why.title: Why add schema markup to your site?

items.title: Win rich results and more clicks in Google
items.body: Valid structured data makes your pages eligible for rich results — star ratings, FAQs, breadcrumbs and more — that take up more space and earn more clicks than a plain blue link.

items.title: Give search engines clearer signals about your content
items.body: Schema removes guesswork. Instead of inferring what your page is about, Google reads exactly what each element is, which helps it index and surface your pages correctly.

items.title: Help AI search understand and cite you
items.body: ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini lean on structured data to parse and trust your content. Clear schema makes your pages easier to quote accurately — more on that below.

whichType.title: Which schema type should you use?
whichType.intro: Match the type to what the page actually is. The most common ones, one line each:

items.name: Article
items.body: for blog posts, news and guides — the default for most content pages.

items.name: FAQ
items.body: for a list of questions and answers, on a help or product page.

items.name: Product
items.body: for an item you sell, with price, availability and reviews.

items.name: Organization
items.body: for your brand — name, logo and social profiles, usually on the homepage.

items.name: LocalBusiness
items.body: for a physical location, with address, phone and opening hours.

howToAdd.title: How to add the markup to your site
howToAdd.body: Wherever your site is built, the JSON-LD goes in the page's head. Copy the block from the tool, then add it using the method for your platform:
howToAdd.h3: WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, or plain HTML

items.body: Paste it into a Custom HTML block, or use an SEO plugin like Rank Math or Yoast that has a schema field.
Add it to your theme's theme.liquid head, or through your theme's structured-data settings.
Open Page Settings → Custom Code and paste the block into the Head section.
Paste the full script block directly inside the head of your HTML file and publish.

bestPractices.title: Schema best practices and common mistakes
dos: Only mark up content that's actually visible on the page.
Fill the recommended fields for a richer, more eligible result.
Use JSON-LD — it's the format Google recommends.
Keep your markup in sync when the page content changes.
Validate before you ship, with the Rich Results Test.
avoids: Marking up content that isn't on the page.
Leaving out the required properties for your type.
Wrong date or URL formats that break validation.
Duplicate or conflicting schema blocks on one page.
Fake reviews or ratings — a fast way to a penalty.

ai.title: Schema markup and AI search

items.title: How ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini use structured data
items.body: AI answer engines parse structured data to understand entities and relationships fast. Clean schema makes your facts machine-readable, so models can extract and attribute them without guessing.

items.title: Structured data and Google's AI Overviews
items.body: AI Overviews pull from pages Google understands well. Schema strengthens that understanding, improving your odds of being one of the sources summarized at the top.

items.title: Why schema is now an AEO and GEO lever, not just SEO
items.body: Answer Engine Optimization and Generative Engine Optimization both reward clarity. Structured data is one of the few signals that speaks directly to machines — making it a lever for AI visibility, not just rankings.

questions.title: Everything you need to know about competitor SEO.
questions.description: Five short chapters on how search rivals win, where gaps usually hide, and how to turn the report into pages that can rank.

items.title: What is SEO competitor analysis?
items.kicker: Read the search results before you write the plan.
items.body: SEO competitor analysis is the practice of studying the domains that already rank for the searches you want. Instead of guessing which pages to build, you look at the topics, keywords, rankings, and content formats that are already collecting demand. The useful output is not a vanity score. It is a clear map of where competitors are strong, where their coverage is thin, and where your site has a realistic chance to win traffic.

items.title: What is a keyword gap analysis?
items.kicker: Proven searches, currently going somewhere else.
items.body: A keyword gap analysis shows the search terms a competitor ranks for and your site does not. These gaps are valuable because the demand is already visible. You are not inventing a topic from scratch; you are finding queries where another page is already earning impressions and clicks. The best gaps often include terms where you are absent, terms where both sites rank but you trail badly, and terms where the current results leave room for a stronger page.

items.title: How do you run an SEO competitor analysis?
items.kicker: From rival domain to a usable content brief.
items.body: Start by choosing true organic competitors: the sites ranking for the queries your customers use, not just the brands you mention in sales calls. Then compare their ranking keywords, traffic estimates, backlink strength, and page types against your own domain. Prioritize the gaps by intent, difficulty, and business value. The final step is turning those gaps into briefs for new pages or updates to existing pages.

items.title: How do you find keyword gaps?
items.kicker: Compare two keyword lists. Keep the useful difference.
items.body: Finding keyword gaps means comparing what your competitor ranks for against what your site ranks for. The priority is not every missing keyword. Focus on searches where the competitor is visible, the intent matches your offer, and the current ranking page is beatable. Thin content, weak topical depth, outdated examples, or a poor match to search intent are signs that a focused page can close the gap.

items.title: How often should you repeat the analysis?
items.kicker: Review before small gaps become durable leads.
items.body: Competitor analysis works best as a recurring habit. A quarterly deep dive is enough for many teams, with lighter monthly checks for new pages and ranking shifts. Search results change as competitors publish, links accumulate, and Google reshuffles the page. The goal is to catch opportunities while they are still open, before a competitor's page becomes harder to displace.

paragraphs: llms.txt is a plain-text file you place at the root of your site (example.com/llms.txt) that gives AI models a curated, structured map of your most important pages. Instead of leaving large language models to guess which URLs matter, it points them to your key content with a short description of each.

As more people search through ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini, being easy for these models to read and cite is becoming part of visibility. A clear llms.txt makes your content simpler to parse and quote, which can help you show up in AI answers rather than getting lost in a noisy crawl.

format.intro: The spec is intentionally simple: a single H1 title, a summary blockquote, and one or more H2 sections of links. Here is a minimal template:
format.sample:
# Your Site Name

> A short summary of what your site is about and who it's for.

## Main
- [Home](https://example.com): What visitors find on the homepage.
- [Pricing](https://example.com/pricing): Plans and what each one includes.

## Documentation
- [Getting Started](https://example.com/docs): How to set things up.

## Optional
- [Terms](https://example.com/terms)
- [Privacy](https://example.com/privacy)

items.title: The required H1 title

paragraphs: Honestly: llms.txt is new, unofficial, and not yet something the major AI providers have confirmed they read at scale. Treat anyone promising guaranteed ranking lifts from it with caution. It's a low-cost, low-risk signal, not a magic switch.

That said, the work it forces is genuinely useful. Writing a clean llms.txt makes you curate your best pages and describe them clearly, which helps any crawler, AI or otherwise, understand your site. As the format gains adoption, having one already in place costs you almost nothing and may help.
Where the real lift comes from is the content itself: pages that clearly answer questions and earn citations. That's the part worth investing in, and it's exactly what our GEO audit measures.

chapters.title: Everything you need to know about H1 tags.
chapters.description: Four short chapters on what the H1 is, how it differs from the title tag, and why search and AI engines lean on it.

items.title: What is an H1 tag?
items.kicker: The headline that frames the whole page.
items.body: The H1 is the main, top-level heading rendered on the page itself — usually the first large line above your opening paragraph. Unlike the title tag, it is visible to readers, and it tells both people and search engines what the page is fundamentally about.

items.title: The H1, the title tag, and H2–H6
items.kicker: Three roles, one clear hierarchy.
items.body: The title tag lives in the document head and shows in the browser tab and search results. The H1 sits on the page as its single main heading. H2 through H6 are subheadings that break the content beneath the H1 into a logical structure.

items.title: How Google and AI engines use the H1
items.kicker: A primary signal of what a page covers.
items.body: Search engines read the H1 as a strong topical signal, matching it against queries to decide what a page is about. A clear, descriptive H1 that includes your primary term early makes that judgment easy — and helps you avoid competing with your own pages.

items.title: H1 tags in AI search and LLM citations
items.kicker: Extra weight where models read and cite.
items.body: In AI-powered search, the H1 does more than rank. As the page's headline it strongly shapes the embedding that represents your content, so LLMs lean on it to summarize and label the page. A descriptive H1 makes your page easier to cite accurately — serving SEO and answer-engine optimization at once.

items.title: One H1 per page
items.description: Use a single H1 so search engines have one unambiguous main heading.

items.title: Length: 20–70 characters
items.description: Long enough to be descriptive, short enough to stay scannable and avoid truncation.

items.title: Include your primary keyword early
items.description: Place the term you are targeting near the start so its relevance is obvious.

items.title: Different from the title tag
items.description: Write a variant of the title tag so the page can target additional related queries.

items.title: Descriptive, not vague
items.description: Tell readers exactly what the page delivers instead of using a generic label.

items.title: Missing H1
items.description: The page has no H1 at all, leaving search engines without a clear main heading.

items.title: Multiple H1 tags on the same page
items.description: More than one H1 splits the signal and muddies what the page is about.

items.title: H1 identical to the title tag
items.description: Duplicating the title tag wastes a chance to target extra queries with a variant.

items.title: H1 too short or too long
items.description: Under 20 characters is rarely descriptive; over 70 gets truncated and loses focus.

items.title: Vague or non-descriptive H1
items.description: Generic headings like "Welcome" tell readers and engines nothing about the page.

whatIsMeta.description: A quick primer for anyone new to the term: where it appears, how it differs from the title tag, and when Google decides to use it.

items.title: Where the meta description shows up in Google
items.body: A meta description is the short snippet in your page's HTML head that search engines show beneath the blue title in results. It never appears on the page itself, but it is the line that tells searchers what to expect before they click.

items.title: The difference between meta description and title tag
items.body: The title tag is the clickable headline; the meta description is the supporting sentence below it. The title states what the page is, while the description makes the case for why someone should open it.

items.title: How Google decides whether to use yours or rewrite it
items.body: Google shows your description when it matches the query well, but rewrites the snippet from on-page text when another passage fits better. A clear, query-relevant description gives it less reason to override you.

items.title: Ideal length: 120-160 characters
items.description: Long enough to be useful, short enough to avoid truncation on both desktop and mobile.

items.title: Include your primary keyword once, early
items.description: Place your target term near the start so Google bolds it and relevance is obvious.

items.title: Lead with value and a call-to-action
items.description: Open with the benefit and add an action verb like discover, learn, or compare.

items.title: One unique description per page
items.description: Write a distinct description for every page so listings never compete or look duplicated.

items.title: Match the search intent
items.description: Speak to what the query is actually looking for so the snippet earns the click.

items.title: Missing or empty meta description
items.description: With no description, Google scrapes a random page passage that rarely sells the click.

items.title: Duplicate descriptions across pages
items.description: Reusing the same description makes listings compete and signals thin, templated content.

items.title: Too long, gets truncated
items.description: Over the pixel limit and Google cuts your sentence off mid-thought with an ellipsis.

items.title: Too short, Google rewrites it
items.description: A few words give Google too little to work with, so it replaces your snippet entirely.

items.title: Keyword stuffing
items.description: Cramming in repeated keywords reads as spam to users and wins nothing with search engines.

items.title: ALL CAPS or awkward formatting
items.description: Shouting capitals and odd punctuation look untrustworthy and can get the snippet rewritten.

aiSearch.ariaLabel: Meta descriptions in AI search and link previews
aiSearch.description: The angle most checkers ignore: your meta description is now read by machines and unfurlers, not just Google.

items.title: How ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini use your meta description
items.body: Answer engines often lift your meta description verbatim when they summarize or cite a page. A sharp, factual description makes your brand easier to quote accurately and harder to misrepresent in AI answers.

items.title: How Open Graph and social link previews work
items.body: When a page is shared on LinkedIn, Slack, or X, the unfurler pulls the Open Graph description, which usually falls back to your meta description. One clear line controls how the link looks everywhere it travels.

items.title: Why one meta description now does double duty for SEO and AEO
items.body: The same sentence has to win the click in Google and feed answer engines and link previews. Writing it once, well, pays off across search, AI, and social at the same time.

chapters.title: Everything you need to know about robots.txt.
chapters.description: Short chapters on what a robots.txt file is, whether to allow AI crawlers, and how it differs from your sitemap.

items.title: What is a robots.txt file?
items.kicker: The first file a crawler reads on your site.
items.body: robots.txt is a plain text file at the root of your domain that tells crawlers which URLs they may request. It controls crawling, not indexing: a blocked page can still appear in search if other pages link to it, so use a noindex tag to truly keep a page out of results. Good crawl rules also protect your crawl budget by steering bots away from low-value URLs like faceted filters and internal search.

items.title: Should you allow or block AI crawlers?
items.kicker: Citations are the new backlinks.
items.body: Our take: allow AI crawlers by default. ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews increasingly send qualified traffic and cite the sources they read, and if you block them you simply won't be in the answer. Avoid one trap: Google-Extended controls Gemini training only and does not affect Google Search, so don't block it thinking you're tidying up Google. Blocking really only makes sense for paywalled or proprietary content you don't want models reproducing for free.

items.title: Robots.txt vs sitemap.xml
items.kicker: One says stay out, the other says come in.
items.body: They are complementary. robots.txt is a blocklist that tells crawlers what not to crawl. sitemap.xml is an invitation, it lists the URLs you do want crawled and indexed, with hints like last-modified dates. Declare your sitemap inside robots.txt so crawlers find it immediately, then keep the two consistent: never disallow a URL you also list in your sitemap.

items.name: User-agent
items.description: Names the crawler the rules below it apply to. Use * to target every bot.

items.name: Disallow
items.description: Blocks a path or folder from being crawled. An empty Disallow allows everything.

items.name: Allow
items.description: Carves out an exception inside a disallowed folder. The most specific rule wins.

items.name: Crawl-delay
items.description: Requests a wait between hits. Bing and Yandex honor it; Google ignores it.

items.name: Sitemap
items.description: Points crawlers to your XML sitemap. Use an absolute URL; it isn't tied to any user-agent.

items.title: Allow all bots (default for most sites)
Block specific AI bots

User-agent: GPTBot

User-agent: CCBot

items.title: Blocking the CSS or JS Google needs
items.description: If you disallow assets used to render the page, Google sees a broken layout and may rank it lower.

items.title: Using robots.txt to hide a page
items.description: Disallow stops crawling, not indexing. To keep a page out of results, use a noindex meta tag instead.

items.title: Disallowing the whole site by accident
items.description: A stray Disallow: / blocks every crawler from everything, the fastest way to vanish from search.

concepts.title: What is AI readability (and how it differs from SEO)?
concepts.description: AI readability is how easily an AI engine can read, understand and quote your page, not how it ranks. SEO gets you found. AI readability gets you cited.

items.title: How AI search reads a page differently from Google's crawler
items.kicker: Google indexes to rank. AI reads to answer.
items.body: Google's crawler maps your page so it can rank it against others. An AI engine pulls the single best answer it can quote, then attributes it. That rewards a clear opening answer and short, standalone facts over raw keyword coverage.

items.title: Readable, understandable, citable: the three levels
items.kicker: Each level builds on the last.
items.body: Readable means the AI can access the text at all. Understandable means it can follow your structure and claims. Citable means it can lift a clean, self-contained answer and trust the source. This tool checks all three.

items.title: AEO and GEO in one sentence
items.kicker: Two names, one goal.
items.body: Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) both mean shaping your content so AI engines pick it as the answer. AI readability is the on-page foundation both rely on.

items.title: Show a named author, sources and a date

items.title: Burying the answer below long intros
items.description: If the answer is in paragraph six, AI will skim past it.

items.title: Walls of text with no structure
items.description: No headings or lists means nothing for AI to map to a question.

items.title: Content rendered only in JavaScript or images

items.title: No schema, no author, no date

items.title: Blocking AI crawlers in robots.txt by accident

items.title: Vague headings that match no real question

chapters.title: Everything you need to know about SERP snippets.
chapters.description: Five short chapters on what a snippet is, the snippet types, why your title and description matter, how pixels beat characters, and what changes in AI search.

items.title: What is a SERP snippet?
items.kicker: The three lines that win or lose the click.
items.body: A SERP snippet is how your page appears in Google's results: the title tag, the URL breadcrumb, and the meta description. Google builds it from your page's HTML, but you supply the raw material. Get it right and you earn the click before a visitor ever lands.

items.title: Organic, paid, rich and featured snippets
items.kicker: Not every result looks the same.
items.body: Organic snippets are the standard free results. Paid snippets are ads marked "Sponsored". Rich snippets add extras like star ratings, dates or prices. Featured snippets lift a direct answer to the very top of the page. This tool previews the organic snippet plus the rich and paid variations through the SERP feature toggles.

items.title: Why your title tag and meta description matter
items.kicker: One is a ranking factor, the other drives clicks.
items.body: The title tag is a direct on-page ranking signal that tells Google what the page is about. The meta description doesn't rank you, but it is your ad copy in the results: a sharp, relevant description lifts click-through rate, which compounds your visibility over time.

items.title: Pixel width vs character count
items.kicker: Google truncates by pixels, not letters.
items.body: Two titles with the same character count can render very differently: a line of W's is far wider than a line of i's. Google cuts your title and description at a pixel budget, so a pixel-accurate preview is the only reliable way to know whether your snippet gets truncated with an ellipsis.

items.title: SERP snippets in AI search and LLM citations
items.kicker: AI Overviews push your snippet down the page.
items.body: AI Overviews now sit above the organic results, pushing your snippet down, and on mobile, well below the fold. At the same time, models like ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini lean on clear titles and descriptions to decide which pages to cite. A precise snippet serves classic SEO and answer-engine optimization at once.

items.title: Title: 50–60 characters, under 600 px
items.description: Long enough to be descriptive, short enough to render in full on desktop without truncation.

items.title: Description: 150–160 characters, under 960 px
items.description: Summarize the page and its value clearly so Google keeps your wording instead of rewriting it.

items.title: Lead with your primary keyword
items.description: Place the term near the start of the title so searchers spot the match instantly.

items.title: Use power words and a clear benefit
items.description: Words like free, guide, or 2026 plus a concrete benefit make your snippet stand out and earn the click.

items.title: Match the search intent of the query
items.description: Write the title and description to answer what the searcher actually wants from that keyword.

items.title: Titles that overflow and get truncated
items.description: Anything past the pixel limit is cut with an ellipsis, often dropping your most important words.

items.title: Descriptions that don't match the content
items.description: If the description oversells or misleads, Google rewrites it and visitors bounce.

items.title: Duplicate titles and descriptions
items.description: Reusing the same tags across pages makes them compete and confuses search engines.

items.title: Keyword stuffing
items.description: Cramming in keywords reads as spam and gets your snippet rewritten automatically by Google.

items.title: Missing meta description
items.description: With no description, Google pulls a random page fragment, usually a poor pitch for the click.

paragraphs: Open Graph is the protocol Facebook introduced in 2010 to control how a URL looks when it's shared. The tags live in your page's head and tell every platform what title, description and image to show instead of guessing.

When the tags are missing, platforms fall back to whatever they can scrape: a random image, the raw title, or nothing at all. Your carefully written post ends up looking like a bare link, and bare links get far fewer clicks.

Almost every major platform reads Open Graph, including Facebook, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack, Telegram and Pinterest. X uses its own Twitter Card tags but falls back to og: when they're absent, so one clean set of tags covers nearly everywhere.

paragraphs: Twitter Card tags (twitter:) are X's own version of Open Graph. When present, they override the matching og: tag on X; when absent, X falls back to og:. So you rarely need a full duplicate set.

In practice, set twitter:card to summary_large_image and let og:title, og:description and og:image do the rest. Add twitter:site or twitter:title only when you want X to show something different from every other platform.

Note the caveat: since 2023, X strips link previews from most free posts and shows a bare link instead. Your tags are still correct, they just may not render there, which is why this tool flags it on the X card.

items.title: og:image missing or too small
items.body: Add an absolute image URL at least 1200x630 and under 500KB. Relative paths and tiny images are the top cause of broken cards.

items.title: Title or description getting truncated
items.body: Keep og:title under 90 characters and og:description under 300. Use the live preview to confirm nothing gets cut off.

items.title: Changes not showing on Facebook or LinkedIn
items.body: Both cache the old preview. Use Facebook's Sharing Debugger (Scrape Again) or LinkedIn's Post Inspector to force a refresh.

items.title: Duplicate or conflicting tags
items.body: Two og:title tags confuse parsers, which may pick the wrong one. Remove duplicates so each tag appears exactly once.

seoImpact.intro: The balanced answer: Open Graph does not directly move Google rankings, but it earns clicks and gives AI crawlers clean context. Here's what it does and does not do.

items.title: What OG does and does not do for ranking
items.body: Open Graph tags are not a direct Google ranking factor. What they do is drive social click-through, which brings real referral traffic and the engagement signals that support rankings indirectly.

items.title: Why clean metadata still helps LLMs read your page
items.body: ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini crawlers use structured metadata to understand what a page is about. Clean og: and title tags give them accurate context to cite you correctly.

items.title: Table stakes, not a growth lever on its own
items.body: Well-formed Open Graph tags are the baseline every professional site should have. They will not rank you alone, but broken tags quietly cost you clicks on every share.

checks.title: What the validator checks
checks.intro: Each rule maps to a part of the llms.txt standard. URL mode runs all of them; pasted text skips the two checks that need an HTTP response.

items.title: File found at /llms.txt
items.body: Confirms your domain returns the file with a 200 response (URL mode only).

items.title: Served as plain text
items.body: Checks the Content-Type header is text/plain, not HTML (URL mode only).

items.title: Valid Markdown
items.body: Makes sure the file parses as Markdown and is not an HTML page or empty.

items.title: H1 title present
items.body: Looks for a single top-level heading naming the site or project. Required.

items.title: Summary blockquote present
items.body: Checks for a short blockquote summary right under the title. Recommended.

items.title: H2 section with a link list
items.body: Verifies you have at least one section with a Markdown list of links.

whatIs.title: What is llms.txt?
paragraphs: llms.txt is a plain-text Markdown file you place at the root of your domain, at /llms.txt. It gives large language models a clean, curated map of your most important pages and a short description of what your site does, so AI tools can understand and cite you more easily.

It is opt-in, and that is the key difference from robots.txt. robots.txt tells crawlers what to stay out of. llms.txt does the opposite: it invites models in and points them at the content you most want represented. Adoption is still early and no major model is confirmed to read it at scale, but the file is cheap to add and easy to keep current.

format.title: The llms.txt format
format.intro: The spec is intentionally simple: one H1 title, an optional summary blockquote, then H2 sections containing Markdown link lists. Here is a known-good template you can copy and adapt.
format.code:
# Your project name
> A one-sentence summary of what your site or product does.

## Docs
- [Quickstart](https://example.com/quickstart): Get up and running fast.
- [Guides](https://example.com/guides): Task-based how-tos.

## API
- [Reference](https://example.com/api): Endpoints and parameters.

## Optional
- [Changelog](https://example.com/changelog): Release notes.

required.title: The required H1 title
required.body: The file must open with a single H1 (# Your project name). This is the one mandatory element, and it tells models what the site is at a glance.

summary.title: The summary blockquote
summary.body: A blockquote (> ...) directly under the title gives a one or two sentence summary. It is recommended, not required, but it greatly improves how models describe you.

sections.title: Link-list sections (and the Optional section)
sections.body: Group your key URLs under H2 headings as Markdown link lists, ideally with a short note after each link. An H2 named Optional marks lower-priority links a model can skip if it is short on context.

fixErrors.title: How to fix common llms.txt errors

items.title: File returns 404 (no file yet)
items.body: You have not published one. Create a file named llms.txt and deploy it to your web root so it loads at https://yourdomain.com/llms.txt.

items.title: Wrong content type (served as text/html)
items.body: Your server is sending the file as a web page. Configure it to return Content-Type: text/plain for /llms.txt, often a one-line rule in your host or framework config.

items.title: Broken links inside the file
items.body: A listed URL 404s or points somewhere stale. Update or remove it, and prefer absolute https URLs so models resolve them correctly.

items.title: Missing title or sections
items.body: Add a single H1 with your site name, then at least one H2 section with a Markdown link list. A summary blockquote under the title is a quick win too.

matters.title: Does llms.txt actually matter?
matters.intro: Here is our honest take. llms.txt is promising and low-effort, but it is not a magic switch for AI visibility. The picture below is balanced on purpose.

confirmed.title: What's confirmed vs still emerging (adoption status)
confirmed.body: The standard exists and a growing number of sites publish one, but no major AI provider has publicly confirmed it reads llms.txt to build answers at scale. Treat support as emerging, not guaranteed.

worth.title: Why a valid file is still worth having (low cost, future-proofing)
worth.body: It takes minutes to write, costs nothing, and cannot hurt you. If and when models lean on it, you are already set up, and it doubles as a clean, human-readable index of your best pages.

necessary.title: Necessary, not sufficient, real AI visibility is the goal
necessary.body: A valid llms.txt is table stakes, not the finish line. Being cited in AI answers comes from authoritative, well-structured content and broad coverage. To see where you actually stand, run a GEO audit.

sections.heading: How to check keyword density
body: Three steps, no signup, and nothing you paste is stored.

subsections.heading: 1. Paste your text or enter a URL
subsections.body: Paste a draft straight from your editor, or switch to URL mode and let the tool fetch the page. In URL mode we strip navigation, footers and comment threads first, so menu labels don't drown out your copy.

subsections.heading: 2. Add your target keywords (optional)
subsections.body: Type the keywords you actually want to rank for, separated by commas. Each gets its own row showing how often it appears, its density, and whether it is missing or pushed into stuffing territory.

subsections.heading: 3. Read the tables, phrases first
subsections.body: The tool opens on the 2-word table on purpose. Single words are noisy; phrases carry topic and intent. Work down from the highest density and ask whether each phrase earns its repetition.

sections.heading: What this keyword density checker shows you
body: Every run returns the same things:
bullets: Total words — the denominator behind every percentage on the page.
Unique keywords — how varied your vocabulary actually is.
Top focus — the single phrase your content leans on hardest.
Stuffing risk — how many separate topics are over-used.
Frequency tables for 1-, 2-, 3- and 4-word phrases, colour-coded by band.
Presence indicators (URL mode) — whether each keyword also appears in your title, meta description and headings.

sections.heading: What is keyword density?
body: Keyword density is how often a word or phrase appears in a piece of content, expressed as a percentage of the total word count. For a single word the formula is simple: divide the number of occurrences by the total number of words, then multiply by 100.

So a word used 12 times in a 600-word article has a density of 2%. For phrases we count the words the phrase actually takes up, because a three-word phrase used 12 times fills 36 words, not 12 — that is 6% of the same article, and it is the honest number for judging whether you are over-doing it.

You will see "keyword density" and "keyword frequency" used interchangeably, but they are not the same measurement. Frequency is the raw count; density is how much of the page that count actually occupies.

sections.heading: What is the ideal keyword density for SEO?
body: There is no magic number, and any tool that gives you one is selling certainty it does not have.

subsections.heading: Why there is no perfect number
subsections.body: Most SEOs work with a rough 1–3% comfort zone, and that is a sanity check rather than a target. Google has never published a density threshold, because density is a symptom, not a ranking factor. Write naturally and you will usually land in that range without trying.

subsections.heading: When a high density is a red flag
subsections.body: Above roughly 5–7%, repetition stops reading as emphasis and starts reading as manipulation. The useful question is never "am I at 2.4%?" but "would a reader notice how often I am saying this?" If a phrase is high because the topic demands it, fine. If it is high because you were hitting a quota, rewrite it.

sections.heading: Keyword density vs keyword frequency
body: Keyword frequency is the raw number of times a term appears. Keyword density is that number divided by the total word count, shown as a percentage.

Frequency tells you what you repeated. Density tells you whether that repetition is proportionate to the length of the page. This tool shows both side by side, because one without the other is misleading.

sections.heading: What is keyword stuffing, and how to avoid it
body: Keyword stuffing is loading a page with repeated terms to influence rankings, at the cost of how it reads. It is one of the oldest SEO tactics and one of the most reliably penalised.

subsections.heading: How Google treats over-optimization
subsections.body: Google's spam policies name keyword stuffing explicitly. The internal Content Warehouse documentation that surfaced publicly in 2024 even included a keywordStuffingScore attribute — a 0-to-127 measure of how stuffed a page looks — a reminder that over-optimization is measured directly, not just a stylistic concern.

subsections.heading: How to fix a stuffed page
subsections.body: Swap repeated phrases for synonyms and natural variations. Bring in related entities — the people, products and concepts a knowledgeable writer would mention anyway — so the page covers the topic instead of hammering the term. Then restructure: a stuffed passage is often two thin paragraphs that should be one good one.

sections.heading: Why phrases matter more than single words
body: A single-word table tells you that "shoes" appears 30 times. That is almost useless on its own — it could be a running shop, a repair guide or a history of footwear.
The 2- and 3-word tables tell you it was "trail running shoes" all along. That is the topic, and it is closer to what people actually search for. Intent lives in phrases, not in individual nouns.

sections.heading: A note on stop words
body: The tool filters common stop words — "the", "a", "of", "and" and their equivalents — from the edges of every phrase. Without that filter the tables fill up with "the best" and "is a", and the report tells you nothing.

It does this per language. A French page gets French stop words, a German page gets German ones, so your tables are not clogged with "de", "la" or "und". Stop words still count toward your total word count — they are just excluded from anchoring a keyword.

sections.heading: Does keyword density still matter in 2026?
body: Less than most tools imply. Modern Google reads synonyms, entities and topic coverage; it does not tally your repetitions and reward a ratio. Density has been a minor, indirect signal for years.

What changed is the second audience. LLMs now sit between your content and a large share of your readers, and they treat stuffed writing the way a human editor would — low quality, hard to summarise, unconvincing to cite.

subsections.heading: From density to topic coverage
subsections.body: The better question is not "how often did I say this?" but "did I cover what someone asking about this needs to know?" Density is a guardrail against over-optimization, not a dial to tune upward.

subsections.heading: What this means for AI search visibility
subsections.body: If you want to know how your pages are actually read by ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini — and whether you get mentioned at all — density will not tell you.

items.question: What is a good keyword density for SEO?
items.answer: There is no official number. Most SEOs treat 1–3% as a comfort zone and anything above roughly 5% as a warning sign. Google has never published a threshold, because density is a symptom of writing quality rather than a ranking factor in itself.

items.question: Does keyword density still matter for SEO in 2026?
items.answer: As a direct ranking factor, barely. Search engines read synonyms, entities and topic coverage rather than counting repetitions. It still matters as a guardrail: a very high density reliably signals over-optimized copy, and both Google and LLMs treat stuffed content as low quality.

items.question: What is the difference between keyword density and keyword frequency?
items.answer: Frequency is the raw count of how many times a term appears. Density is how much of the page those occurrences take up, shown as a percentage — so a three-word phrase counts for three words each time it appears. A phrase used 12 times is unremarkable in a 2,000-word guide and excessive in a 200-word description.

items.question: Can I check keyword density for a URL?
items.answer: Yes. Switch to URL mode and enter any publicly accessible page. The tool fetches it, strips navigation, footers and comment threads, then counts only the body content. Private or login-walled pages are not supported.

items.question: Does this tool work for non-English content?
items.answer: Yes. The language is detected automatically and the matching stop-word list is applied, so a French, German or Spanish page is analyzed with its own function words filtered out. It also handles languages that do not separate words with spaces, such as Chinese, Japanese and Thai.

items.question: Is this keyword density checker free?
items.answer: Yes, completely free with no signup. We also never store the text you paste, so you can safely check unpublished drafts.

faqs.question: What exactly is the whitelabel solution?
faqs.answer: You resell our platform under your own brand. Your clients see your logo, your domain and your colours across the whole dashboard, with nothing indicating that BabyLoveGrowth powers it behind the scenes.

faqs.question: What are my two options for working with you?
faqs.answer:
Whitelabel — the platform runs on your domain with your branding. Setup is free, and you pay {perWebsitePrice} per website with bulk discounts. Your clients log in to your branded dashboard.

Direct onboarding (Grow plan) — you onboard clients through our platform at {perWebsitePrice} per website with bulk discounts. You handle the CMS integrations and the content appears on your clients' sites without them needing dashboard access.

faqs.question: What does the whitelabel plan cost?
faqs.answer: Setup is free. You pay {perWebsitePrice} per website per month, the same as our standard pricing, with bulk discounts as you add websites. There are no other fees.

faqs.question: How long does setup take, and what do you need from me?
faqs.answer: You set it up yourself in a few minutes. We need a domain or subdomain you own — for example app.yourbrand.com or platform.youragency.com — the ability to change its DNS settings, and your logo and brand colours. We show you the DNS records to add, and your domain connects as soon as they resolve, usually within minutes but up to 48 hours with some providers.

faqs.question: What branding do my clients see?
faqs.answer: Your custom domain, your logo throughout the dashboard, and your brand colours and styling — from the sign-in screen to every page inside. Our branding is removed completely, so clients never see that another platform powers the solution.

faqs.question: What can my clients see and do in the dashboard?
faqs.answer: You onboard clients exactly as you would normally; the difference is that the credentials you share open a dashboard on your domain. There they review their content plan and published articles, the backlinks given and received, the technical audit and their Search Console analytics.

faqs.question: Two of my clients are in the same niche. Will they get the same articles?
faqs.answer: No. Keyword research, clustering and brand voice are set per client site, so each plan is built from that client's own niche, audience and competitors — even where the topics overlap.

faqs.question: Can each client have their own tone, audience and language?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the default. Tone of voice, target audience, competitors, content language and CMS credentials are configured per client site, and you switch between clients from one dashboard.

faqs.question: Which option should I choose?
faqs.answer: Choose whitelabel if client dashboard access under your brand matters to how you sell, or if owning a branded platform is part of your business model. Choose direct onboarding if you would rather manage everything yourself and your clients simply want results on their website.

faqs.question: What happens if a client leaves?
faqs.answer: Cancel that client site at any time; the rest of your roster keeps running untouched. You only pay for active client websites.

faqs.question: Do you support my clients directly?
faqs.answer: No — the platform is whitelabeled under your brand, so you keep the client relationship. We provide partner support to help you resolve anything technical.

faqs.question: Can I move from direct onboarding to whitelabel later?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can upgrade at any time, and setup is free.

items.question: How can you afford to pay me and write for free?
items.answer: BabyLoveGrowth is a paid SEO platform. Our subscribers need high-quality, contextual backlinks to grow their own sites. We write articles for your blog as part of that service — each one includes 1–2 links to subscriber content. Subscribers pay for their plan, you get free articles and a share of the revenue. Everyone wins.

items.question: What exactly appears on my site?
items.answer: A full SEO article on a topic your audience searches for. It includes 1–2 contextual links to vetted, relevant sites from our network, plus internal links back to your existing posts. It reads like something you'd publish yourself.

items.question: Do I have to write or edit anything?
items.answer: No. We pick the topic, write the article in your voice, and publish it. If you want to review articles first, turn on approval mode — nothing goes live until you say so.

items.question: Will this hurt my rankings?
items.answer: No. We check every topic against your Search Console data so a new article never competes with pages you already rank for. What lands is a useful post on a search you weren't covering, with a couple of natural outbound links.

items.question: How and when do I get paid?
items.answer: Your Domain Rating in dollars, per article. Once we confirm the article is live, your rate gets added to your balance. Payouts land in your Stripe account monthly — no invoice, no minimum payout.

items.question: What happens if a link is removed?
items.answer: We monitor links after publishing. If one disappears, we'll ask you to restore it. Sites that consistently remove links stop receiving new articles.

items.question: Is it really free?
items.answer: Yes. No subscription, nothing to pay. You don't need a BabyLoveGrowth plan to participate.

items.question: Which platforms work?

metadata.title: BabyLoveGrowth MCP — Connect Claude to Your SEO Data
metadata.description: The BabyLoveGrowth MCP server plugs Claude into your live Search Console and GA4: quick wins, AI-search traffic, decaying pages, cannibalization and a full site health check. What MCP is, how to connect, and the top 6 prompts.

hero.title: Plug Claude into your <highlight>SEO data.</highlight>
hero.description: One URL turns Claude into your SEO analyst. Connect the BabyLoveGrowth MCP server and Claude reads your live Search Console and GA4 — quick wins, AI traffic, decay, cannibalization and a full site health check — all read-only, nothing published or changed.

whatItIs.title: One protocol, <highlight>zero plumbing</highlight>
whatItIs.description: MCP is how Claude talks to the outside world. Instead of pasting exports into a chat, you give Claude one secure connection to your data and it does the rest.

cards.title: An open standard
cards.description: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that lets Claude connect to outside tools and data through a single URL — no plugins, no scripts, no copy-pasting CSVs.

cards.title: Read-only and secure
cards.description: You sign in with your own Google account and pick which property to share. Access is read-only — Claude can read your data, but nothing is ever published or changed.

cards.title: Your live data
cards.description: Every answer runs against your real Search Console and GA4 in real time — not a stale export from last week. Ask a question, get the current numbers back.

enables.title: Everything Claude can <highlight>read for you</highlight>
enables.description: Once connected, Claude can pull all of this on demand or on a schedule — no SEO tool to log into, just ask.

groups.title: Search Console intelligence
items: Quick wins — queries ranked 5–15 with real impressions, the fastest path to page 1
Top queries and pages, clicks, impressions, CTR and average position
Keyword cannibalization — where two of your URLs compete for the same query
Decaying pages and traffic drops, ranked by the clicks you’re losing
Country breakdown for any query or page

groups.title: Analytics & AI traffic
items: Traffic overview and trends from GA4 — sessions, users, conversions
Channel breakdown — organic, direct, referral, paid and social
AI search traffic — visits from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude
Top landing pages by traffic and engagement

groups.title: Technical & GEO audit
items: Health score and Core Web Vitals / page-speed signals
llms.txt, robots.txt and sitemap presence for AI crawlers
On-page issues — schema, canonicals, H1s, meta and broken links
A prioritized fix list Claude writes for you, highest impact first

comparison.title: BabyLoveGrowth vs <highlight>other SEO MCP servers</highlight>
comparison.description: Most SEO MCPs are data-API wrappers or self-hosted open-source projects. This one plugs Claude into your own live Search Console and GA4 — free, in one URL.
comparison.footnote: DataForSEO provides third-party API data with no connection to your own Search Console. Open-source SEO MCPs vary by project and are typically self-hosted.

connect.title: How to connect Claude in <highlight>eight steps</highlight>
connect.description: Paste one URL into Claude, sign in with your own Google account, and every prompt below runs against your live data — read-only, nothing is published or changed. Skip Google and you still get the free AI search strategy for your website.

steps.title: Add a custom connector
steps.caption: In Claude (Desktop or claude.ai), open Settings → Connectors, click Add, and choose Add custom connector.
steps.alt: Claude Connectors settings with the Add menu open on “Add custom connector”

steps.title: Paste the MCP URL
steps.caption: Name it BabyLoveGrowth, paste the MCP URL above, and click Continue.
steps.alt: Add custom connector dialog with the BabyLoveGrowth MCP URL pasted in

steps.title: Keep the detected settings
steps.caption: Claude detects the sign-in settings on its own — leave both marked Detected as they are and click Add.
steps.alt: Authentication and OAuth client options with the detected defaults selected

steps.title: Click Connect
steps.caption: Open the new connector and hit Connect to start the secure handshake.
steps.alt: BabyLoveGrowth connector screen with a Connect button

steps.title: Sign in with Google, or skip
steps.caption: Grant read-only access to Search Console and Analytics. It can read, never publish or change — and no BabyLoveGrowth account is needed. Only want the free AI search strategy? Click Skip, just get the free report.
steps.alt: Connect Claude screen with a Connect Google account button and a Skip, just get the free report button

steps.title: Pick your property
steps.caption: If you connected Google, choose the Search Console and/or GA4 property Claude should read, then Authorize. Pick at least one — both gives the fullest picture.
steps.alt: Choose your data screen selecting a Search Console and Analytics 4 property

steps.title: Check it connected
steps.caption: The connector now lists its SEO tools. Leave them on Needs approval and Claude will ask before each one — every prompt below runs on your live data. If you skipped Google, it lists only the free report tool.
steps.alt: Connected BabyLoveGrowth connector listing its SEO tools and permissions

steps.title: Get your free AI search strategy
steps.caption: Ask Claude to “create AEO strategy to make website yoursite.com first on ChatGPT for all buying prompts”. In about a minute you get your AI visibility for one buyer question, a 30-day content plan, the technical issues on your homepage and a first article with a cover image, plus a PDF of everything. Each website gets one free report.
steps.alt: 30-day content plan calendar from the free AI search strategy report

connect.footnote: Custom connectors work on any Claude plan, including free (the free plan allows one custom connector).

prompts.title: Copy, paste, <highlight>run on your data</highlight>
prompts.description: Six prompts that work the moment you’re connected — each reads your live data and hands back a clear set of actions to run this week.
prompts.playbookCta: See the full Claude SEO prompt playbook

items.title: Quick-Win Finder
items.description: Reads your connected Search Console and surfaces the rankings Google already half-trusts — the fastest wins on your site this quarter.
items.prompt: Read my Search Console for the last 28 days. List queries ranked 5–15 with 200+ impressions, sorted by position × impressions. For each: the ranking URL, current CTR, and the single on-page change to make.

items.title: AI Search Visibility
items.hook: See where ChatGPT & Perplexity send you
items.description: Pulls your GA4 AI-referral traffic so you can see which pages ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude actually cite — and where you’re invisible.
items.prompt: Show my traffic from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude over the last 90 days. Which landing pages do they send visitors to, how is it trending, and which money pages get zero AI traffic today?

items.title: Decaying-Page Rescue
items.hook: Catch traffic loss before it compounds
items.description: Finds pages whose clicks are sliding or that dropped versus the previous period, ranks them by the traffic at risk, and tells you the likely cause.
items.prompt: Find my decaying pages and biggest traffic drops versus the previous 90 days. Rank by clicks lost, and for the top 10 tell me the likely cause and the one fix to recover each.

items.title: Cannibalization Fixer
items.hook: Stop your own URLs from competing
items.description: Spots queries where two or more of your pages fight for the same ranking, then tells you which to consolidate, redirect or differentiate.
items.prompt: Find keyword cannibalization in my Search Console — queries where two or more of my URLs rank for the same term. For each, recommend whether to consolidate, redirect or differentiate, and which URL should win.

items.title: Technical + GEO Audit
items.hook: A prioritized fix list in one prompt
items.description: Runs a full technical and GEO audit on your site — health score, page speed, llms.txt, schema and on-page issues — and hands back a fix list ranked by impact.
items.prompt: Run a technical and GEO audit on my homepage. Report the health score, page speed, and whether llms.txt, robots.txt and sitemap are present, then list on-page and schema issues as a fix list prioritized by impact.

items.title: LLM Visibility Checker
items.hook: See how often AI models mention you
items.description: Runs an LLM visibility test across Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity, then builds a clean HTML dashboard — overall mention rate, the per-provider breakdown, the brands winning the answers and a prioritized fix list.
items.prompt: Run an LLM visibility test for my site using the BabyLoveGrowth MCP, then build an HTML dashboard visualizing the result: a donut chart of overall mention rate, a bar chart of mention rate by provider (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity), a horizontal bar chart ranking the top mentioned brands with ours highlighted, a table of each prompt with per-provider mention status (✓/✗), a table of domain stats (organic keywords, traffic, top 10 keywords, AI Overview references), and a prioritized table of recommendations (technical + content) sorted by priority. Use a clean, modern style with green = mentioned, red = not mentioned.

items.question: What is an SEO MCP server?
items.answer: An SEO MCP server connects your AI assistant to real SEO data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) — the open standard that lets tools like Claude call external services. Instead of pasting CSV exports into a chat, Claude fetches your live Search Console and GA4 numbers itself, every time you ask.

items.question: Is the BabyLoveGrowth MCP free?
items.answer: Yes. Paste the URL into Claude and sign in with Google — no BabyLoveGrowth account, no API keys, no credit card. Custom connectors work on every Claude plan, including free.

items.question: Which AI assistants does it work with?
items.answer: Any client that supports remote MCP servers. The guide above covers Claude (Desktop and claude.ai), and the same URL works in tools like Cursor or ChatGPT connectors.

items.question: What SEO data can I access?
items.answer: Live Search Console data (queries, pages, clicks, positions, quick wins, cannibalization, decaying pages), GA4 traffic including AI-search referrals from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude, and a technical + GEO audit of any page on your site.

items.question: Is it safe to connect my Google account?
items.answer: Access is read-only and scoped to the property you pick during sign-in. Claude can read your data but never publish or change anything, and you can revoke access at any time from your Google account settings.

items.question: Do I need coding knowledge to set it up?
items.answer: No. Setup is pasting one URL into Claude’s connector settings and signing in with Google — about two minutes, no API keys or config files.

items.question: How is this different from a traditional SEO tool?
items.answer: A dashboard shows you charts and leaves the analysis to you. Connected over MCP, Claude reads the same live data and does the analysis — it finds the quick wins, explains the drops and hands back a prioritized action list you can question in plain English.

items.question: What are the limitations?
items.answer: It’s read-only by design — Claude can analyze but never change your site. Data comes from your own Search Console and GA4, so there’s no third-party keyword database, and Claude can only see properties you’ve connected.

cta.description: Paste the MCP URL into Claude, sign in with Google, and run the prompts above on your own live data — no BabyLoveGrowth account required.
